GDF15 impacts chronic kidney disease and associated weight loss through distinct mechanisms
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Mitochondrial and Epigenomic Medicine, Cardiovascular Institute, and Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia; Philadelphia, PA, USA.; Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine.; Institute of Diabetes Obesity and Metabolism, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania; Philadelphia, PA, USA.; Cardiovascular Institute, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania; Philadelphia, PA, USA.
items.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is frequently accompanied by anorexia, cachexia, and inflammation, which collectively contribute to poor clinical outcomes. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we demonstrate a pivotal role for growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) in CKD morbidities. Deteriorating renal function and clinical disease status correlates with GDF15 levels in plasma and kidneys of CKD patients. In a mouse CKD model, GDF15 levels are elevated and Gdf15 knockout ( Gdf15 −/− ) mice are partially protected from CKD-induced anorexia and weight loss despite worsening renal function and inflammation. GDF15 receptor Gfral knockout ( Gfral −/− ) mice recapitulate these phenotypes. Metabolic cage studies reveal that the weight loss-protection effects are primarily attributed to increased food intake. Intriguingly, pair-fed Gdf15 −/− and Gfral −/− mice exhibited phenotypic and molecular divergence. Pair feeding in Gdf15 −/− mice reverses loss-of-GDF15’s effect on body weight but does not restore renal functions. In contrast, pair feeding in Gfral −/− mice reverses loss-of-GFRAL’s effect on both body weight and renal function. Transcriptome analysis suggests that GDF15 may act through both GFRAL-dependent mechanisms on food intake and GFRAL-independent mechanisms that primarily modulate inflammation and metabolic pathways. A monoclonal antibody that neutralizes circulating GDF15 markedly restores food intake and preserves body weight, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of targeting GDF15 in CKD-associated weight loss. Together, these findings demonstrate GDF15-GFRAL as a potential therapeutic target for CKD-associated weight loss and suggest GFRAL-dependent, food intake-mediated actions of GDF15 and food intake-independent effects that may contribute to renal inflammation and metabolic regulation.

items.title: The circSRSF5 -FUS-EIF4A3 regulatory circuitry protects Ewing sarcoma cells from EWS::FLI1 small-molecule inhibition
items.last_author_affiliation: Life-Istituto di Ricerca e Cura-Santa Lucia IRCCS, Laboratory of Molecular and Cellular Neurobiology, Via del Fosso di Fiorano, 64, 00143 Rome, Italy.; University of Rome “Foro Italico,” Department of Movement, Human, and Health Sciences, Piazza Lauro de Bosis, 6, 00135 Rome, Italy.
items.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have become a key focus in cancer research due to their high stability, diversity, and ability to regulate various biological processes. This study explores the impact of small-molecule inhibition of EWS::FLI1 oncogene by YK-4-279 in Ewing sarcoma (ES). ES is a rare and highly aggressive childhood cancer driven by fusion proteins that disrupt normal gene regulation and promote tumor growth. Current treatments rely on intensive chemotherapy with serious long-term side effects, emphasizing the need for targeted therapies. A promising new approach targets the interaction between EWS::FLI1 and the RNA helicase DHX9 through the small molecule YK-4-279, which displays strong antitumor effects and has advanced to clinical trials. Transcriptome profiling revealed widespread changes in circRNA expression after YK-4-279 treatment, with a notable up-regulation of circSRSF5 . Functional and mechanistic evidence identifies a key role for circSRSF5 in tumor cell survival by stabilizing the anti-apoptotic protein eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4A3 (EIF4A3) and contributing to therapy resistance. These findings uncover a previously unidentified role for circRNAs, particularly circSRSF5 , in ES pathogenesis and treatment response.

items.title: Multimodal motion and behavior switching of multistable ciliary walkers
items.last_author_affiliation: AMOLF, Science Park 104, Amsterdam 1098 XG, Netherlands.; Institute for Complex Molecular Systems and Department of Mechanical Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology, P.O. Box 513, Eindhoven 5600 MB, Netherlands.
items.abstract: The collective motion of arrays of cilia—tiny, hairlike protrusions—drives the locomotion of numerous microorganisms, enabling multimodal motion and switching between gaits to navigate complex environments. Inspired by this multimodal motion, we introduce multistable soft walkers with millimeter-scale flexible cilia that buckle under the walkers weight, coupling multistability and actuation within a single physical mechanism. When placed on a vibrating surface, the propulsion direction of ciliary walkers is selected through the buckled states of their cilia, allowing multimodal motion and switching between modes in response to perturbations. We first show that bimodal walkers with left-right symmetric cilia can reverse direction upon encountering obstacles. Next, we demonstrate that walkers with isotropic cilia exhibit both translational and rotational motion and switch between them in response to environmental interactions. At increasing densities, swarms of such walkers collectively transition from predominantly spinning to translational motion. Last, we show that the shape, placement, and number of cilia controls the modes of motion of the walkers. Our results establish a rational, physically grounded strategy for designing minimalist soft robots where complex behaviors emerge from feedback between internal mechanical states and environmental interactions, laying the foundation for soft robotic collectives that operate without onboard sensing or centralized control.

items.title: Signals of rapid genetic change in reef coral over time and following mass mortality
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Integrative Biology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin TX, USA.
items.abstract: Future coral reef persistence amidst accelerating climate change depends on rapid adaptive capacity. Sixteen years (2003 to 2019) of genetic data ( N = 903) spanning mass mortality events uncovered polygenic signals of evolution and population structure in one Great Barrier Reef coral species ( Acropora tenuis ) and a similar but nonsignificant trend in another ( Acropora millepora ). Random forest revealed larger genetic shifts postbleaching compared to other time points, which was further supported by critical transitions in 34 years of remotely sensed thermal data (1985 to 2018). Concordant signals across multiple genomic ordinations confirmed significant shifts postbleaching. Specifically, three genetic variants contributed significantly to key random forest splits over time in A. tenuis . Significant genome-wide covariance in allele frequencies suggests shifts due to selection, not drift. This suggests that coral gene pools are changing, and measurable evolution can happen over subdecadal timescales, giving hope for coral resilience amid the ongoing climate crisis. However, we caution against overoptimism, and stress emissions must be urgently reduced.

items.title: Rapid intensification of summer convective precipitation in New England
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Earth, Environmental, and Planetary Sciences, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA.
items.abstract: Anthropogenic warming is intensifying precipitation extremes, yet how subdaily convective rainfall responds in historically stratiform-dominated midlatitude regions remains poorly constrained. Using four decades of hourly station observations and reanalysis data, we show that summer convective precipitation has intensified across much of New England and surrounding regions from 1980 to 2020, with high-intensity events increasing in higher latitudes. Extreme convective rainfall scales at ∼13 to 14% per degree Celsius, nearly twice the Clausius-Clapeyron rate and significantly faster than stratiform precipitation. This intensification is accompanied by shorter event durations, increased moisture convergence, enhanced convective instability, and reduced antecedent soil moisture. Our results indicate a warming-driven shift toward convective dominance linked to changes in midlatitude circulation, reduced meridional temperature gradient, and land-atmosphere coupling, placing New England within an emerging poleward extension of the summer convective regime.

items.title: Misremembered social networks are predictions of the future in disguise
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Sociology, University of South Carolina, Columbia, SC, USA.
items.abstract: Mistakes in how the brain processes social network information in the present can predict the network’s future state.

items.title: Probabilistic neural code for subjective value and metacognition in human cortex
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Psychology, The Ohio State University, Columbus, OH 43201, USA.
items.abstract: Subjective value underlies many everyday decisions, yet the neural representations supporting these valuations are inherently noisy and subject to uncertainty. Whether humans have metacognitive access to this uncertainty and how this access is supported neurally remain unclear. Here, we provide converging behavioral and neural evidence that subjective value is represented probabilistically in the human brain. Behaviorally, participants’ uncertainty reports tracked trial-by-trial fluctuations in valuation. Neurally, we decoded probability distributions over value from functional magnetic resonance imaging activity in ventromedial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex, and superior parietal lobe and intraparietal sulcus. Decoded neural uncertainty predicted behaviorally reported uncertainty across trial, item, and individual levels. Moreover, predicting behavioral uncertainty required modeling the covariance structure of population noise. These findings indicate that neural populations jointly encode value and uncertainty, extending probabilistic population coding from perception, working memory to subjective value, and providing a neural basis for metacognitive access to uncertainty in value-based decisions.

items.title: From genetic risk factor to therapeutic target: The CREB3L4-GDF15 axis drives prostate cancer immune evasion
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Urology, Zhongda Hospital, Southeast University, Nanjing 210009, China.; Basic Medicine Research and Innovation Center of Ministry of Education, Zhongda Hospital, National Innovation Platform for Integration of Medical Engineering Education (NMEE) (Southeast University), State Key Laboratory of Digital Medical Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing 210009, China.
items.abstract: Advanced prostate cancer (PCa) is characterized by rapid progression and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, contributing to poor clinical outcomes and limited therapeutic responses. Mendelian randomization (MR) uses genetic variants as instrumental variables to assess causal associations while minimizing confounding and reverse causation. Through integrative proteogenomic analysis, including MR and colocalization across 438,178 males, we identified CREB3L4 as associated with PCa risk. CREB3L4 overexpression promoted tumor growth in mice, accompanied by activation of cholesterol metabolism, androgen receptor (AR) signaling, and immunosuppression. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed CREB3L4 enrichment in human PCa cells. Interaction analysis identified enhanced growth and differentiation factor (GDF) signaling in CREB3L4 + tumor cells, with CD8 + T cells as the primary receivers. Ligand–receptor analysis and coculture experiments identified GDF15 as the key mediator, through which tumor cells suppressed CD8 + T cell proliferation and activation via TGFBR2 signaling. In vivo, GDF15 neutralization attenuated CREB3L4-driven tumor growth and CD8 + T cell dysfunction, whereas prostate-specific CREB3L4 knockout or adeno-associated virus-mediated knockdown suppressed tumor growth and restored CD8 + T cell function. Clinical analyses confirmed elevated CREB3L4 and GDF15 expression in PCa, inversely associated with CD8 + T cell infiltration and immunotherapy response. Collectively, these findings reveal that CREB3L4 promotes AR signaling-mediated GDF15 expression, driving CD8 + T cell dysfunction and identifying the CREB3L4–GDF15 axis as a potential therapeutic target in PCa.

items.title: Aclarubicin disrupts RNA polymerase II progression at replication-coupled histone genes
items.last_author_affiliation: Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, Seattle, WA 98109, USA.; Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Chevy Chase, MD 20815, USA.
items.abstract: Anthracyclines are effective chemotherapeutic agents that cause DNA and chromatin damage. One member of the anthracyclines, aclarubicin, has gained therapeutic interest due to its ability to kill cancer cells through chromatin-based mechanisms, thus avoiding the off-target effects associated with DNA damage. However, the molecular mechanism of action leading to aclarubicin-induced chromatin damage remains elusive. Here we performed Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) and other transcriptional regulators in human cells following aclarubicin treatment. We found that aclarubicin strongly disrupts the replication-coupled histone genes, resulting in a nonproductive accumulation of Pol II transcription machinery at levels exceeding those at other genes. We attribute this sensitivity to the dense Pol II loading and rapid transcription of the histone genes, which intensify the chromatin-disrupting effects of aclarubicin. Together, our findings shed light on the mechanism of aclarubicin as an anticancer drug and point to the replication-coupled histone genes as a target for therapeutic intervention.

items.title: Surface-passivated high-entropy oxide-derived catalysts for stable dry reforming of methane
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Chemistry, Institute for Advanced Materials and Manufacturing, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, TN 37996, USA.; Chemical Sciences Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, TN 37831, USA.
items.abstract: Dry reforming of methane (DRM) enables the co-valorization of CO 2 and CH 4 into syngas, yet the development of sintering- and coking-resistant catalysts that suppress CH 4 cracking while accelerating coke gasification without compromising reaction efficiency remains a major challenge. Here, we address this challenge by employing surface-passivated catalysts derived from high-entropy oxides (HEOs) for stable DRM operation. Alkaline earth metal cation (M 2+ )-doped HEOs were designed to function without pretreatment and exhibited resistance to sintering and coking. This robustness arises from the in situ exsolution of NiCuCo alloy nanoparticles encapsulated within a multifunctional BaCO 3 overlayer, enabled by HEO-stabilized Ba incorporation and Ba-mediated surface reconstruction during DRM. This adaptive architecture passivates deep CH 4 cracking, promotes CO 2 activation, accelerates coke gasification, and thereby sustains catalytic efficiency and durability. Comprehensive spectroscopic, microscopic, and diffraction analyses revealed the structural dynamics and mechanistic pathways governing catalyst evolution under DRM conditions.

items.title: Evolution of trans-regulatory architecture and gene expression dosage compensation after genome duplication
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Animal and Aquacultural Sciences, Section for Genome Biology, Faculty of Biosciences, Norwegian University of Life Sciences, 1433 Ås, Norway.
items.abstract: Whole-genome duplication (WGD) through polyploidization has played a major role in genome evolution across eukaryotes. While many well-studied WGDs involve allopolyploidization, autopolyploidization provides a distinct context because duplicated chromosomes initially originate from within the same species and retain high sequence similarity. A major consequence of WGD is the rewiring of gene regulatory networks, partly driven by selection on gene expression dosage. In multicellular organisms, evidence for dosage balance selection has relied largely on comparative patterns of duplicate gene retention and expression, with few studies directly examining regulatory architecture after WGD. Here, we analyzed a large-scale eQTL dataset from Atlantic salmon ( Salmo salar ), which experienced a salmonid-specific autopolyploid WGD approximately 80 to 100 million years ago. We found that trans-regulatory connections were preferentially retained between WGD-derived syntenic regions and that syntenic trans-eQTL pairs showed elevated three-dimensional genomic contact, suggesting partial preservation of spatial proximity between duplicated chromosomal regions. Overall, 230 duplicated gene pairs (5%) shared eQTLs, suggesting conserved regulatory control. Moreover, 16 gene pairs showed genotype-dependent compensatory expression effects mediated by a common regulator, consistent with predictions of the dosage balance hypothesis. These gene pairs were significantly enriched in late-rediploidizing regions. Our results indicate that a small subset of duplicated genes have retained dosage-balanced regulatory architecture long after WGD.

items.title: Resolving topological obstructions to vectorial structured field control
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford, Parks Road, Oxford OX1 3PJ, UK.
items.abstract: The use of structured matter, such as optical retarders, for vectorial control is a well-established and widely used technique in modern optics, and has driven continued advances in the manipulation of complex, spatially varying vectorial fields. However, achieving arbitrary field conversion typically requires the use of cascaded elements, as intrinsic physical and fabrication constraints fundamentally limit individual devices to a restricted subset of transformations. This results in an overall continuous transformation potentially failing to be continuous at the level of the parameters of the cascade, leading to detrimental engineering consequences such as the introduction of complex, discontinuous aberrations that disrupt important topological properties of the underlying light and matter fields. In this work, we establish a mathematical framework for analyzing the topological difficulties that emerge in the decomposition of an overall transformation into individual layers, and for determining the minimal depth required to overcome them. The strategy introduced provides a general pathway for optimizing designs for vectorial field control and matter field generation, with particular importance for the manipulation of topological phases in optical polarization fields, such as Stokes skyrmions, where continuity is of vital importance.

items.title: Atomic-scale visualization and assignment of contaminant adsorption geometries at mineral surfaces
items.last_author_affiliation: Center for Environmental Systems, Department of Civil, Environmental and Ocean Engineering, Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ 07030, USA.
items.abstract: Directly resolving coexisting adsorption geometries at mineral-water interfaces and assigning them to crystallographic sites remains challenging in environmental geochemistry. Ensemble methods provide population-averaged structural constraints but may obscure minor or similar configurations and do not directly reveal crystallographic registry. Here, we establish an experimentally constrained framework integrating controlled off-axis high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM), multislice simulations, and density functional theory (DFT) to resolve crystallographic adsorption registries and corresponding structures. For selenium(IV) adsorption on hematite (001), comparison of apparent selenium positions with multislice simulations accounting for tilt-induced registry shifts supports assignment to iron-iron bridge and oxygen-centered hollow registries. DFT favors monodentate inner-sphere structures compatible with these registries. Extension to lead(II) and uranium(VI) on multiple hematite facets demonstrates the transferability of the off-axis imaging strategy for resolving sparse high- Z interfacial species. This work enables real-space, site-resolved adsorption-structure analysis that complements ensemble-averaged structural methods and provides a basis for mechanistic models of contaminant retention and structure-guided sorbent design.

items.title: Tuning microswimmer motility by liposome encapsulation: A membrane clutch enables controlled swimming and cargo transport
items.last_author_affiliation: Graduate School of Engineering Science, The University of Osaka, 1-3 Machikaneyama, Toyonaka, 5608531, Japan.
items.abstract: Inspired by biology’s use of vesicles for targeted transport, many studies have propelled liposomes with active matter, creating synthetic systems that can be viewed as microscale biohybrid robots. Nevertheless, the underlying motility mechanisms from a hydrodynamic perspective are often unresolved, and reliable velocity control remains challenging. In the present study, we use our previously introduced biohybrid system termed the chlamylipo, in which the motile alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is encapsulated within a giant liposome, as a model system to investigate how liposome encapsulation regulates microswimmer motility under controlled perturbations. From a fluid mechanical perspective, we establish a deformation-velocity expression that incorporates liposome radius, beating frequency, and membrane protrusion. We further show that motility can be reversibly switched by incorporating light-responsive lipids, with the liposome acting as a “clutch” that modulates membrane protrusion. To demonstrate its transport function, we further show cargo loading, carrying, and triggered release. These results show that liposome encapsulation can convert a motile microorganism into a controllable carrier, with the membrane acting as a clutch that regulates swimming and, therefore, cargo transport.

items.title: A flexible fiber–based artificial chemical postsynapse
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Advanced Materials Science & Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Gyeonggi 16419, Republic of Korea.; SKKU Advanced Institute of Nanotechnology (SAINT), Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Gyeonggi 16419, Republic of Korea.; Samsung Advanced Institute for Health Sciences & Technology (SAIHST), Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Gyeonggi 16419, Republic of Korea.; Biomedical Institute for Convergence at SKKU (BICS), Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon, Gyeonggi 16419, Republic of Korea.
items.abstract: Most artificial synapses, which are designed to communicate with biological neural systems and exhibit neuron-like functions, rely primarily on electrical signals. Biotic-abiotic neural interfaces that use artificial synapses to communicate with biological synapses via chemical neurotransmitters while exhibiting synaptic plasticity are of great interest. Here, we present an artificial chemical postsynapse that directly interfaces with biological systems through dopamine (DA) neurotransmitters and demonstrates synaptic plasticity–like behavior. The artificial postsynapse of a flexible fiber–based organic electrochemical transistor (F-OECT) with a capacitive-like charging gate electrode, which combines volumetric charge storage and DA-sensing functionalities, can detect pulsatile DA release and transduce these sensing signals with plasticity-like behavior. The F-OECT synapse emulates key synaptic functions observed in biological synapses by responding to pulse-like DA release from dopaminergic cells. We also implanted fiber-based artificial postsynapses into a mouse brain to study their basic interaction with DA release and to evaluate biocompatibility.

items.title: Umbilical cord structure shapes feto-maternal heat transfer across mammals
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Mathematics, University of Manchester, Manchester M13 9PL, UK.; Maternal and Fetal Health Research Centre, University of Manchester, Manchester M13 9WL, UK.
items.abstract: The umbilical cord varies widely across placental mammals, yet the functional consequences of this structural diversity remain unclear. We compared cord anatomy across 130 mammal species, reconstructed ancestral states, and combined multimodal imaging with physics-based modeling of oxygen and heat transfer. Reconstructions indicate that the ancestral umbilical cord was uncoiled, with three vessels and an allantoic duct; the human combination of coiling with loss of the duct is rare. Across species, vessel number, duct persistence, and cord length increase with birth weight. Modeling predicts that oxygen delivery remains near maximal across architectures but that placental heat loss depends more strongly on umbilical flow and on cord length and coiling, suggesting more efficient cooling in larger mammals. Microscopy and ultrasound imaging reveal geometric vessel layouts, including a human triple helix, consistent with configurations predicted to reduce intervessel heat shunting. As fetuses must dissipate heat through the mother, these results link cord morphology, evolution, and fetal thermal resilience.

items.title: Skeletal muscle proteomics reveals metabolic phenotype–specific adaptations to exercise training in health, obesity, and type 2 diabetes
items.last_author_affiliation: Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research, Faculty of Health and Medical Sciences, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark.
items.abstract: Exercise training improves metabolic health, including whole-body insulin sensitivity, yet the molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. We applied proteomics and phosphoproteomics to skeletal muscle biopsies from lean men, and men with obesity or type 2 diabetes (T2D), obtained before and after 8 weeks of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) under basal and insulin-stimulated conditions. Before HIIT, protein expression showed a stepwise progression from lean to obesity to T2D. HIIT induced more pronounced proteomic remodeling in obesity and T2D compared with lean men, characterized by increased mitochondrial and decreased proteasomal contents. Phosphoproteomic responses were diagnosis dependent, revealing distinct insulin signaling adaptations. Mechanistically, AMP-activated protein kinase γ2 (AMPKγ2) emerged as a prominent HIIT-regulated protein, exhibiting increased incorporation into AMPKα2β2 complexes across all phenotypes, and AMPKγ2 overexpression in human myotubes increased basal glucose oxidation. These findings elucidate molecular pathways underlying exercise-induced insulin sensitization and suggest AMPKγ2 as a candidate regulator for exercise-induced metabolic adaptation.

items.title: Mantle redox states reveal contrasting styles of late Archean lithospheric subduction
items.last_author_affiliation: Key Laboratory of Geological Processes and Mineral Resources, School of Earth Sciences and Resources, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, PR China.; School of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ 85281, USA.
items.abstract: Lithospheric recycling has operated through most of Earth’s history, likely involving subduction since the late Archean. However, the thermal structure and geometry of such subduction systems remain poorly constrained. Here, we quantify the oxygen fugacity ( f O 2 ) of mantle sources modified by recycled supracrustal materials in the North China Craton. By integrating mantle f O 2 estimation, thermodynamic simulation of lithospheric structures, and other geological constraints, we infer two styles of lithospheric subduction with contrasting slab-dip angles. The dominant style shows shallow slab-dip angles, a more reduced arc mantle and a thick overriding lithosphere. The subsidiary, localized style exhibits relatively steep slab-dip angles, a more oxidized mantle source and a thinner overriding lithosphere. In contrast to the prevalence of steep subduction on the modern Earth, flat (or shallow) subduction profoundly shaped the distinctive tectonic evolution of the early Earth, whereas the localized development of steep subduction may have enhanced mantle oxidation and strengthened coupling between Earth’s deep interior and surface environments.

items.title: DAS reveals continuous, multicore architecture of the Alpine Fault, New Zealand
items.last_author_affiliation: Te Kura Tātai Aro Whenua School of Geography, Environment and Earth Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington Te Herenga Waka, Wellington 6012, New Zealand.
items.abstract: The Alpine Fault accommodates much of the relative motion between the Australian and Pacific plates in southern New Zealand and is expected to produce large earthquakes in coming decades. How slip evolves and what ground motions are produced during the next rupture are expected to depend strongly on the continuity of principal slip zones and overall fault width. Despite extensive study, the along-strike structure of the fault and its continuity across segment boundaries remain poorly constrained. Here, we use distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) along a 30-kilometer fiber-optic array crossing the Alpine Fault to record fault-zone guided waves (FZGWs) from local earthquakes. The FZGW observations, supported by numerical modeling and passive seismic imaging, reveal up to six narrow (∼10 meters) fault cores embedded within a 200-meter-wide low-velocity zone interpreted as the fault’s inner damage zone. The principal fault core feature persists for ∼180 kilometers along strike between the Central and South Westland segments, crossing a pronounced geometric and kinematic boundary. The inferred damage zone width is consistent with empirical scaling for large-displacement faults. These results demonstrate that DAS can resolve fault-zone architecture at previously inaccessible scales and bridge geological and geophysical inferences, providing constraints on fault continuity, slip localization, and the potential for multisegment rupture in mature plate-boundary systems.

items.title: A divergent bat orthopneumovirus with zoonotic potential constrained by RSV adaptive immunity and broad-spectrum treatment
items.last_author_affiliation: Institute of Virology, Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, corporate member of Freie Universität Berlin and Humboldt Universität zu Berlin, Berlin 10117, Germany.; German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), associated partner Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Berlin 10117, Germany.
items.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; genus Orthopneumovirus ) causes severe pneumonia in young children worldwide, yet the zoonotic potential of the few known nonhuman animal orthopneumoviruses remains unknown. Here, we characterized a highly divergent bat orthopneumovirus (BPV) from West African straw-colored fruit bats and established a systematic framework for evaluating zoonotic risk posed by an emerging viral pathogen. Epidemiologic data in bats showed a low viral detection rate (24 of 1778 RT-PCR positive) and low seroprevalence (6 of 66 IgG IFA positive), suggesting BPV episodic circulation potentially sustained in immunologically naïve bats following bat birthing events. Near-complete genomes from two BPV genetic variants revealed prototypic orthopneumovirus organization, but lacked the SH viroporin-encoding gene present in RSV. Functional experiments showed that BPV NS1/NS2 antagonized human interferon β responses, and that BPV pseudoviruses entered human cells (4.5- to 53.5-fold less efficiently than RSV), while being cross-neutralized by human RSV-reactive antisera, together suggesting zoonotic traits that may be partly constrained by cross-protective immunity. BPV escaped neutralization by RSV-specific therapeutic palivizumab and inhibition by lonafarnib, but remained susceptible to MPE8, a broad-spectrum monoclonal antibody that targets the conserved pneumovirus antigenic site III. These findings identify zoonotic traits of a divergent bat pneumovirus while suggesting potential protective value of preexisting RSV immunity and broad-spectrum interventions, which has implications for pandemic preparedness. Whether cross-protection in the human population may change by the advent of RSV vaccination warrants investigation. Efforts to investigate orthopneumovirus host shifts, reservoir studies, and development of broadly reactive orthopneumovirus vaccines and antivirals are warranted.

items.title: Errors in social network knowledge predict how ties evolve in the future
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Cognitive and Psychological Sciences, Brown University, Providence, RI 02906, USA.; Carney Institute for Brain Science, Providence, RI 02906, USA.
items.abstract: A notable feature of people’s social knowledge is that it is riddled with errors. These errors, e.g., making mistakes about who are actually friends in a social network, has typically been attributed to cognitive limitations or heuristics that prioritize knowledge of general social patterns over details about specific ties. Here, we demonstrate that such errors instead reflect an adaptive link prediction process that anticipates how the network will evolve far into the future. By longitudinally following a large, real-world social network ( n = 196) and tracking the formation and dissolution of social ties over the course of a year, we show that judgments that are wrong in the moment accurately forecast which relationships will emerge or dissolve up to 6 months later. On average, participants’ errors predicted tie formation nearly 3× and tie loss more than 1.2× above chance levels. Beyond the use of simple heuristics like triadic closure and homophily, computational modeling reveals that successful link prediction relies on mental representations of the social network that integrates information about both direct and indirect, long-range ties between individuals. Having a social network representation that is future-oriented yields distinct social advantages: Those who are better able to predict changes in the network become more centrally positioned over time, contingent on their initial position.

items.title: Hybrid transverse thermoelectric conversion based on off-diagonal Peltier and Ettingshausen effects in a junction-less single material
items.last_author_affiliation: National Institute for Materials Science, Tsukuba 305-0047, Japan.; Department of Advanced Materials Science, Graduate School of Frontier Sciences, The University of Tokyo, Kashiwa 277-8561, Japan.
items.abstract: Transverse thermoelectric conversion, which interconverts heat and charge currents in orthogonal directions, is gaining attention as a driving principle for next-generation thermal management devices that do not require dissimilar material junctions or complex module structures. Transverse thermoelectric conversion is driven by various principles stemming from the breaking of structural symmetry or time-reversal symmetry, and substantial performance improvements are anticipated by simultaneously utilizing multiple principles. This study demonstrates hybrid transverse thermoelectric conversion based on multiple phenomena within a junction-less single material. Using an active thermoelectric imaging technique based on lock-in thermography, the charge-to-heat current conversion characteristics in Mg 3 Bi 2 crystals showing anisotropic transport properties were visualized and evaluated. We successfully separated the contributions of the off-diagonal Peltier effect due to the electronic structural symmetry breaking and the ordinary Ettingshausen effect due to the time-reversal symmetry breaking under a magnetic field. These contributions operate additively within the same material, leading to the notable enhancement of the transverse thermoelectric conversion performance.

items.title: Characterizing ocean flows with the scattering transform
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA.
items.abstract: Upper-ocean flows are a complex multiscale jigsaw puzzle of turbulence and waves. Characterizing these flows is essential for understanding their role in redistributing heat, carbon, and nutrients. While power spectral analysis offers a useful statistical descriptor of these flows, it cannot always distinguish between different types of motion. We show that the scattering transform (ST), a wavelet convolution method, can extract geometric information from flow fields, offering insights beyond the power spectrum. The ST distinguishes balanced dynamics, internal waves, and different flavors of geophysical turbulence—even when their power spectra are identical. Applied to sea surface height (SSH) fields from ocean models, the ST differentiates regions with distinct underlying dynamics. Our analysis offers a framework for interpreting SSH from satellite altimetry and for analyzing other spatial maps (e.g., from airborne and coastal radar). More generally, the ST is an appealing way to characterize complex fluid motion in a variety of contexts.

items.title: Ubiquitination of USP5 by a bacterial effector inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory for Diagnosis and Treatment of Severe Zoonotic Infectious Diseases, Key Laboratory for Zoonosis Research of the Ministry of Education, College of Veterinary Medicine, Jilin University, Changchun, China.
items.abstract: The intracellular pathogen Legionella pneumophila employs a repertoire of effector proteins to manipulate the host ubiquitin signaling and subvert host immune responses. In this study, we reported that the L. pneumophila effector GobX (Lpg2455) functions as a ubiquitin ligase to target the host deubiquitinase USP5. Ubiquitination of USP5 by GobX inhibits its deubiquitination activity. Furthermore, this ubiquitination enhances the interaction between USP5 and the host E3 ligase MARCHF7, thereby facilitating MARCHF7-dependent ubiquitination of NLRP3. This modification targets NLRP3 for autophagic degradation, ultimately suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation in macrophages. Our findings uncover a sophisticated strategy in which a bacterial effector hijacks the host ubiquitination machinery to dampen inflammasome signaling.

items.title: Multimodal robotic matter enabled by unified magnetic control primitives
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA.; Princeton Materials Institute (PMI), Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA.
items.abstract: Robotic matter seeks to achieve collective functionality through interactions among modular units governed by global control signals. A persistent challenge is identifying control frameworks that are simultaneously scalable and deterministic. Here, we introduce a unified magnetic control paradigm that enables multimodal robotic matter using a minimal set of global-field primitives. We show that combinations of rotating and pulsed uniform fields, together with controlled field gradients, are sufficient to generate diverse behaviors—including multimodal locomotion, deterministic bottom-up assembly, and rapid, reversible shape morphing in origami-inspired modular robots. Each module incorporates permanent magnets with prescribed chirality and magnetic moment, encoding mechanical and magnetic asymmetries that map global field inputs to predictable forces, torques, and deformation pathways. Using a programmable three-dimensional Helmholtz coil system, we demonstrate four locomotion modes (rolling, steering, sliding, and walking), hierarchical assembly of three-dimensional robotic architectures, and millisecond-timescale transitions among discrete stable states, with applications to origami state machines and global shape change for navigation through confined spaces. By unifying locomotion, assembly, and reconfiguration within a single control framework, this work establishes a generalizable approach to magnetic robotic matter in which multifunctional collective behaviors emerge from a minimal set of control primitives.

items.title: Global iodine emissions remain near constant over the 21st century
items.last_author_affiliation: Wolfson Atmospheric Chemistry Laboratories, Department of Chemistry, University of York, York YO10 5DD, UK.
items.abstract: The reaction between atmospheric ozone and ocean iodide releases gaseous iodine into the atmosphere, destroying ozone and nucleating aerosol particles. The current paradigm is that iodine emissions will substantially increase over this century, with implications for climate, air quality, and human health. Using advanced predictions of ocean iodide concentrations and the iodine emissions function, we re-evaluate this understanding. Rather than increasing through 2100, we find minimal change (−3%) in global iodine emissions compared to present day, predominantly due to a sea surface temperature driven decrease in the iodine emissions function together with relatively unchanged sea surface iodide concentrations. However, emissions increases remain in the critical Arctic region (+143%), resulting in an additional 9 ppbv of springtime surface ozone loss across the region. Our results highlight that predictions of future atmospheric iodine depend on the assumed climate-induced changes in oceanic iodide, in addition to changes in emissions driven by anthropogenic ozone and sea-surface temperature.

items.title: A programmable cell-free biosensor device for on-demand detection of pathogens and antibiotics
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Advanced Drug Delivery and Release Systems, School of Pharmacy, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310058, China.; Department of General Surgery, Sir Run-Run Shaw Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, 310016, China.; Jinhua Institute of Zhejiang University, Jinhua 321299, China.; Liangzhu Laboratory, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 311121, China.; MOE Key Laboratory of Macromolecular Synthesis and Functionalization, Department of Polymer Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China.; Institute of Fundamental and Transdisciplinary Research, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, 310009, China.
items.abstract: Cell-free systems provide a versatile platform for engineering customizable, gene circuit-based biosensors for decentralized, low-cost molecular diagnostics. Nevertheless, their performance in complex samples is often compromised by matrix interference, necessitating laborious preprocessing that restricts field deployment. Here, we developed a programmable, on-demand, cell-free kit (POCKit) that integrates sample pretreatment with point-of-care detection. The POCKit device comprises a negative pressure storage chamber and a sampling-sensing chamber, which can be connected to a microneedle array or pipette module for sample collection, filtration and target detection via a freeze-dried cell-free molecular reaction network. The POCKit enables detection of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in wound exudates, interstitial fluids and artificial sputum within one hour. It also detects tetracycline in food and environmental water, distinguishing tetracycline-spiked samples from negative controls without specialized equipment or tedious preparation. A portable fluorescence imaging box and smartphone application further support real-time signal acquisition and analysis, offering a ready-to-use platform for on-site diagnostics across biomedicine, food safety, and environmental monitoring.

items.title: Cryo-EM reveals a transmembrane allosteric site and activation mechanism for the SERCA calcium pump
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biochemistry, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta T6G 2H7, Canada.
items.abstract: Impaired sarco-endoplasmic reticulum Ca 2+ -ATPase (SERCA) activity contributes to defective calcium handling and cellular dysfunction in cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, yet the structural basis of small-molecule SERCA activation has remained unknown. SERCA is a ubiquitous P-type ATPase that restores cytosolic Ca 2+ to the sarco-endoplasmic reticulum and is essential for cardiac Ca 2+ cycling and cellular energy homeostasis. Here, we used cryogenic electron microscopy to define how two chemically distinct activators, CDN1163 and UM-52, enhance SERCA function. Structures at 2.6 Å and 3.1 Å resolution show that both compounds bind the same previously unrecognized activation hotspot in the transmembrane domain, a shallow groove formed by helices M3 and M4 and capped by M1. Despite limited chemical similarity, both activators share conserved interactions with Ser265 and Trp272 and stimulate Ca 2+ -dependent ATPase activity. Activator binding promotes a catalytically competent, calcium-bound E1-like conformation of SERCA that may involve altered protein-lipid interactions. These findings establish a structural framework for rational design of potent next-generation SERCA activators.

items.title: Spaceflight reshapes Alzheimer’s disease–associated molecular programs in human brain organoids
authors: Juliana de S. da G. Fischer
items.last_author_affiliation: Integrated Space Stem Cell Orbital Research Center, Sanford Stem Cell Institute, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA.; Department of Pediatrics and Cellular & Molecular Medicine, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA.
items.abstract: Spaceflight provides a unique environment to study neural responses relevant to neurodegenerative diseases. Here, human cortical organoids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells that carry familial Alzheimer’s disease (AD) mutations in APP, PSEN1 , and PSEN2 were cultivated at the International Space Station alongside Controls for 40 days. Multiomic profiling, integrating transcriptomics and proteomics, revealed a coordinated shift in neuronal and cellular states during spaceflight. Spaceflight was associated with changes in amyloid-β processing and tau phosphorylation, although the magnitude of these responses varied across genetic backgrounds. Pathway analysis identified increased synaptic and neurotransmission-related signatures, particularly those associated with GABA-releasing and glutamatergic signaling. Integrative analysis further revealed convergent programs involving RNA processing, chromatin organization, cytoskeletal dynamics, and cellular stress responses. Proteomic and multiomic analyses also identified changes in RNA binding proteins, including CIRBP, consistent with altered posttranscriptional regulatory networks under spaceflight conditions. These exploratory findings indicate that spaceflight reshapes neuronal regulation in human brain organoids, revealing coordinated molecular responses relevant to AD biology.

items.title: How far are we from a critical salinity in the North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre?
items.last_author_affiliation: Environnements et Paléoenvironnements Océaniques et Continentaux (EPOC), UMR CNRS 5805, EPOC-OASU Université de Bordeaux, Pessac, France.
items.abstract: The North Atlantic Subpolar Gyre (SPG) can undergo abrupt cooling associated with a loss of deep convection, yet the hydrographic conditions that drive this transition remain uncertain. While some CMIP6 models simulate an abrupt SPG cooling, others do not. Here, we identify a critical sea surface salinity (SSS) that separates these contrasting behaviors. Models without abrupt cooling either remain above this threshold because they project weak freshening or already lie below it under present-day conditions, inconsistent with observations. Observed SSS exceeds the critical threshold by 0.3 to 0.8 g kg −1 , depending on the exact threshold definition. Although no declining trend is currently detected, observations remain consistent with models that simulate abrupt cooling. In these models, SSS begins to decline rapidly and crosses the critical threshold about 20 years after the onset of freshening. These results highlight the importance of sustained salinity observations for detecting the approach to this critical threshold, providing a physically based early warning of an abrupt SPG cooling.

items.title: Selenium isotopes uncover the mechanism of the deep plate tectonic cycle in the MORB mantle
items.last_author_affiliation: Instituto Andaluz de Ciencias de la Tierra (IACT-CSIC), CSIC, Armilla, Granada, Spain.
items.abstract: Subduction has recycled oceanic crust into Earth’s interior for billions of years, yet how deeply subducted material evolves and contributes to mantle-derived melts, such as mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORBs), remains poorly resolved. Because subducting slab-derived dehydration fluids typically produce isotopically light selenium (Se) in residual eclogites, which is transferred to mantle melts without further fractionation, Se serves as a powerful isotope-based tracer of recycled components into the mantle. Here, we present high-precision Se isotope data for recycled crust–derived garnet pyroxenites that bridge the gap between the primitive mantle and isotopically lighter MORB. Through two-stage thermodynamic modeling, we trace the reactive infiltration of eclogite-derived melts within the convective mantle, leading to the concurrent formation of subduction-derived garnet pyroxenites that preserve residual eclogite cores, both of which contribute to the mantle source of MORBs during adiabatic decompression. Our results establish a petrologically consistent and isotope-validated framework to trace the fate of subducted crust and its long-term imprint on the MORB mantle throughout the deep plate tectonic cycle.

items.title: Hardware-encoded modality separation for multimodal sensing and artificial perception
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea.; Department of AI Systems Engineering, Sungkyunkwan University, Suwon 16419, Republic of Korea.
items.abstract: Human skin achieves robust perception by distributing modality-specialized receptors that preferentially encode mechanical and thermal cues. Yet, soft and flexible tactile sensors often suffer from cross-sensitivity, where stretching, bending, and temperature variations generate overlapping electrical readouts that undermine reliable multimodal measurement and downstream artificial intelligence–based interpretation. Here, we present a multimodal piezoresistive platform based on doped silicon nanomembranes that leverages their crystallographic anisotropy and a bilayer differential architecture for front-end modality separation. By integrating [110] longitudinal/transverse gauges with [100] reference gauges that exhibit reduced piezoresistive sensitivity but comparable temperature coefficient of resistance, together with a bilayer differential layout, the platform compensates thermal drift and decouples stretching from bending at the hardware level. Experimental and theoretical analyses establish a quantitative framework for separating modality-specific responses under combined stretching, bending, and temperature stimuli. Integrated into a flexible, wireless platform, the decoupled signals enable real-time transmission and deep learning–based interpretation, allowing accurate identification of geometrically similar objects with distinct thermal or mechanical properties. These results highlight the feasibility and need to co-design front-end sensing architectures and learning models to achieve robust, high-accuracy multimodal decoupling in real-world conditions.

items.title: Stress unmasks disconnected endocrine coordination of glucose metabolism in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Biological Sciences, University of Canterbury, Christchurch 8041, New Zealand.; Biomolecular Interaction Centre, School of Biological Sciences, University of Canterbury, Christchurch 8140, New Zealand.; Department of Medicine, University of Otago, Christchurch 8014, New Zealand.; Maurice Wilkins Centre for Molecular Biodiscovery, Auckland 1010, New Zealand.
items.abstract: Skeletal muscle orchestrates systemic metabolism, dynamically coordinating glucose uptake and fuel use to match energy demand. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), loss of dystrophin is associated with altered metabolic regulation. Using physiological stress to unmask metabolic deficits in the mdx mouse model of DMD, we show that stress hormone signaling rises without an appropriate poststress rise in insulin secretion, maintaining hyperglycemia despite elevated basal glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. Rather than reflecting increased gluconeogenesis, this hyperglycemia appears to stem from impaired glucose oxidative disposal; skeletal muscle stores glucose as glycogen instead of oxidizing it, while the heart and brain show persistent, tissue-specific uptake differences. Restoring insulin availability transiently corrects glucose control and reverses stress-induced deficits. Instead of correcting glucose handling, removing excess glucose directly using empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor) prevents stress-induced increases in blood glucose. These findings identify a breakdown in endocrine-metabolic coordination underlying metabolic vulnerability in DMD and demonstrate two mechanistically distinct routes, restoring insulin secretion or bypassing it entirely, to restore metabolic resilience under stress.

items.title: A precipitation threshold delineates contrasting controls on global soil pH under nitrogen fertilization
items.last_author_affiliation: School of Environmental Science & Technology, Tianjin University, Tianjin, 300072, China.
items.abstract: Nitrogen fertilization is a major driver of soil acidification globally, yet its independent effects on soil pH and the underlying mechanisms remain poorly resolved. Here we isolate the contribution of nitrogen fertilization by compiling the largest paired experimental dataset to date, consisting of 3564 paired soil pH observations under control and nitrogen fertilization treatments across seven major ecosystem types worldwide. By constructing robust machine-learning models, we predict global soil pH under nitrogen fertilization (pH_T) and quantify fertilization-associated pH change under a standardized hypothetical fertilization scenario. Under this scenario, we estimate that 96.27% of global soils undergo acidification, with a mean pH decline of 0.34 units. Critically, we identify a precipitation threshold at ∼900 mm year −1 that separates two distinct regimes in the relationship between precipitation and pH_T: climate-driven leaching and buffering in drier regions versus soil-mediated internal regulation in humid regions. This threshold demonstrates that the association between precipitation and pH_T is not uniform across the global precipitation gradient but varies markedly among hydroclimatic regions. Our results provide a global outlook on soil pH responses to nitrogen fertilization, supporting acidification risk early warning, precision fertilizer management, and sustainable agricultural development.

items.title: Visual learning through auditory reactivation during wakefulness and sleep
items.last_author_affiliation: Key Laboratory of Brain, Cognition and Education Sciences, Ministry of Education, South China Normal University, 510631 Guangzhou, China.; School of Psychology, South China Normal University, 510631 Guangzhou, China.; Center for Studies of Psychological Application, Guangdong Key Laboratory of Mental Health and Cognitive Science, South China Normal University, 510631 Guangzhou, China.; Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory of Reading and Development in Children and Adolescents, Ministry of Education, South China Normal University, 510631 Guangzhou, China.
items.abstract: Visual learning, like other kinds of learning, has classically been attributed to intensive, active training; however, whether it can be achieved via effortless, passive reactivation remains unresolved. Here, we triggered targeted reactivation using auditory tones that had acquired contextual meaning through preceding visual–auditory associative learning. Re-exposure to learned tones improved subsequent visual performance during both wakefulness and slow-wave sleep. Wake reactivation matched training in both improvement and improvement per trial, whereas sleep reactivation surpassed both wake reactivation and training. By contrast, re-exposure to unlearned tones impaired performance only during slow-wave sleep. Reactivation-induced improvement and impairment were strictly orientation- and location-specific and were associated with a convergent auditory–visual coupling pathway. Beyond this shared pathway, auditory reactivation during wakefulness and sleep unfolded through distinct coupling architectures linking sensory and higher-order cortical regions. Collectively, our findings establish auditory reactivation as a highly efficient route to visual learning, identify sleep as its most potent state, and reveal a double-edged, state-dependent neuroplastic architecture.

items.title: Historical evidence that wildfire frequency modulates debris-flow hazards through sediment-supply limitation
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA.
items.abstract: Southern California is an epicenter of postwildfire debris flows. In this region, steep topography, frequent fire, heavy rainstorms, and large populations along the wildland-urban interface conspire to produce costly debris flows. Wildfire frequency in the region has tripled in recent decades, causing concern about escalating debris-flow hazards. Here, we investigate how wildfire frequency affects the magnitude of postfire erosion by analyzing long-term debris basin records. We identify two contrasting erosional styles. In steep catchments, erosion exhibits a binge-purge behavior: Erosion for 3 years following fire exceeds background rates by ∼17×. In contrast, in low-sloping, soil-mantled catchments, sediment export following fire only exceeds background rates by ∼1.5×. Critically, in the steep catchments, debris-flow volumes decline when wildfires recur more frequently than the ∼30-year interval characteristic of the past century. This observation suggests a sediment-supply limitation in which more frequent wildfire may reduce, rather than amplify, some of Southern California’s most severe debris-flow hazards.

items.title: Bioinspired mucolytic microrods for active mucus penetration and enhanced antibiotic delivery against H. pylori
items.last_author_affiliation: Australian Institute for Bioengineering and Nanotechnology, University of Queensland, Brisbane, QLD 4067, Australia.; Drug Delivery, Disposition and Dynamics, Monash Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Monash University, Parkville, VIC 3052, Australia.
items.abstract: Helicobacter pylori infects half of the global population and is a major driver of gastric cancer. Clinical eradication remains challenging because antibiotics must survive the acidic gastric lumen, penetrate the viscoelastic mucus barrier, and reach bacteria residing near the gastric epithelium. Here, we report a biomimetic oral delivery system that integrates rod-shaped morphology, acid protection, active mucolysis, and localized antibiotic delivery. The platform consists of clarithromycin-loaded Santa Barbara Amorphous-15 silica microrods coated with a pH-responsive alginate-pronase conjugate. The coating protects clarithromycin and pronase under acidic gastric conditions, while the less acidic inner mucus microenvironment promotes coating detachment and pronase-mediated mucolysis, enabling active mucus penetration. In vitro and in vivo studies show that these bacteria-mimicking microrods significantly enhance mucus penetration and increase gastric residence time twofold. In a murine infection model, the platform achieved 100% eradication at 15 milligrams per kilogram and maintained 90% clearance at 7.5 milligrams per kilogram, producing a ∼2000-fold bacterial burden reduction compared to free clarithromycin. This bioinspired, shape-guided strategy offers a promising paradigm for localized gastrointestinal therapy.

items.title: Arctic forcing of European spring productivity and agricultural yields linked to Barents Sea ice loss
items.last_author_affiliation: International Institute for Earth System Science, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu 210023, China.; Jiangsu Provincial Key Laboratory for Advanced Remote Sensing and Geographic Information Technology, Key Laboratory for Land Satellite Remote Sensing Applications of Ministry of Natural Resources, School of Geography and Ocean Science, Nanjing University, Nanjing, Jiangsu 210023, China.
items.abstract: Arctic sea ice loss reshapes midlatitude climate, yet its cascading impacts on terrestrial carbon cycling and food security remain unclear. Barents Sea ice area (BSIA) has experienced the Arctic’s fastest decline. Using four decades of satellite observations, agricultural statistics, and Earth system model (ESM) simulations, we identify late-winter BSIA as a key driver of European spring productivity. Interannual BSIA reductions substantially enhance gross primary productivity (GPP) and raise national wheat yields by up to 16.5% in Eastern Europe, a global breadbasket. Reanalysis and model experiments reveal that reduced BSIA alters large-scale circulation through stratosphere-troposphere coupling, wave–mean flow interactions, and Rossby wave propagation. Anomalous subsidence drives adiabatic and radiative warming; cyclonic flow strengthens warm-air advection, together alleviating thermal constraints on photosynthesis. Although most ESMs capture atmospheric teleconnections, they systematically underestimate productivity responses due to underrepresented GPP-temperature sensitivity. BSIA decline accounts for approximately half of the four-decade increase in Eastern European productivity, highlighting an overlooked Arctic forcing of midlatitude carbon dynamics.

items.title: Continuously aligned biomimetic sites in MXene membranes for rapid lithium extraction
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Urban-rural Water Resource and Environment, Harbin Institute of Technology, 73 Huanghe Road, Nangang District, Harbin, China.
items.abstract: Efficient separation of lithium ions (Li + ) from magnesium ions (Mg 2+ ) remains a central challenge for direct lithium extraction from salt lake brines due to their similar physicochemical properties. Inspired by biological ion channels, biomimetic membranes have been explored to improve Li + /Mg 2+ separation. However, most biomimetic membranes focus primarily on introducing recognition sites while overlooking the structural features of biological channels, particularly the continuous arrangement of coordination sites that facilitates efficient ion transport. Here, inspired by the continuous carbonyl coordination structure of the KcsA ion channel, 4-formylbenzo-15-crown-5 ether was periodically grafted onto poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) chains and integrated with MXene nanosheets to construct two-dimensional interlayer channels with continuously aligned crown ether recognition sites. This architecture shifts Li + transport from random diffusion to successive site-to-site hopping, reducing the effective transport energy barrier. The resulting biomimetic MXene membrane achieves a Li + flux of 0.12 mol·m −2 ·h −1 with Li + /Mg 2+ selectivity of 109 and performs effectively across various salt lake brines.

items.title: Unseen but not unheard: Animal-borne audio recorders reveal missing interactions between seabirds and untracked vessels
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biology, University of Oxford, Life and Mind Building, Oxford OX1 3EL, UK.
items.abstract: Quantifying interactions between marine megafauna and vessels is key to assessing the ecological impacts of commercial fishing and shipping. Automatic identification systems (AIS), by publicly tracking global vessel activities, have enabled animal-vessel interactions to be identified at scale. However, the extent of these interactions is inevitably underestimated due to “unseen” vessels that lack AIS or have gaps in coverage from technical issues or intentional disabling. Using animal-borne audio recorders on three seabird species (northern gannet, Balearic shearwater, and Westland petrel), we investigated whether acoustic detection of vessel sounds could reveal a more complete picture of interactions. We found that a striking proportion of vessel audio detections (gannets, >32%, estimated 57%; shearwaters, >12%, estimated 20%) could not be matched with AIS-tracked vessels, suggesting substantial potential for bycatch risk from unseen fishing. Our approach is computationally lightweight, applicable to pre-existing datasets, and transferrable to non-seabird taxa. Acoustic detection could improve future assessments of animal-vessel interactions and unseen vessel activities to support marine conservation.

items.title: Ultra-generalized hologram synthesis via domain-adaptive wavefront learning
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Precision Measurement Technology and Instruments, Department of Precision Instrument, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China.
items.abstract: Deep learning–based computer-generated holography is essential for creating lifelike three-dimensional (3D) visuals in extended reality and immersive human-digital interaction. However, current data-driven approaches predominantly rely on a 3D-solution search strategy that couples scene representation with physical parameters. This paradigm leads to physical overfitting, restricting models to fixed wavelengths and depths and preventing generalization across diverse 3D data formats. Here, we report a 2D-solution search technique, wavefront-aware neural encoding (WNE). This method is a universal framework that overcomes these limitations via domain-adaptive wavefront learning. By compensating for feature distribution shifts induced by varying data formats and physical parameters, WNE maps various wavefronts into a unified feature domain compatible with a frozen, pretrained encoder. This mechanism enables ultra-generalized hologram synthesis: A single pretrained network can encode high-fidelity phase-only holograms for diverse 3D representations, from conventional layer-based data to emerging Gaussian splatting. Outperforming previous analytical and neural encoding methods in image quality, WNE establishes a robust, plug-and-play engine for diverse holographic applications.

items.title: TREX1 and TREX2 3′ → 5′ DNA exonucleases enhance the fidelity of translesion synthesis by DNA polymerase θ
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston, Galveston, TX 77555, USA.
items.abstract: A multiplicity of translesion synthesis (TLS) DNA polymerases (Pols) promote replication through DNA lesions in an error-free or error-prone manner. Among these Pols, Polθ operates in an error-prone manner. However, Polθ conducts TLS in human cells in a much more error-free manner than implicated from the high error-proneness of the purified Pol. To resolve this incongruity, here we show that the TREX1/TREX2 3′ → 5′ exonucleases are integral components of TLS mediated by Polθ. In TREX1- or TREX2-deficient cells, Polθ-dependent TLS becomes nonoperational and chromosomal instability rises similar to that in Polθ-deficient cells. Consequently, similar to that in Polθ −/− mice, trex2 −/− mice exhibit increased susceptibility to ultraviolet-induced skin cancers. Furthermore, our findings that in the absence of TREX1/TREX2 3′ → 5′ exonuclease activities, Polθ-mediated TLS manifests high mutagenicity, and an increase in the diversity of misincorporated nucleotides demarcate a crucial role of these exonucleases in the removal of Polθ misinsertions and, thereby, in enhancing Polθ TLS fidelity and the consequent genome stability.

items.title: Uterine-derived anisotropic compressive force specifies the anterior-posterior axis orientation in the mouse embryo
items.last_author_affiliation: Division of Embryology, National Institute for Basic Biology, Okazaki, Aichi 444-8787, Japan.; Basic Biology Program, SOKENDAI (The Graduate University for Advanced Studies), Okazaki, Aichi 444-8787, Japan.; Laboratory for Animal Resources and Genetic Engineering, RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research, Kobe, Hyogo 650-0047, Japan.
items.abstract: The establishment of the anterior-posterior (A-P) axis is a fundamental process in embryonic patterning. In mice, directional migration of the anterior visceral endoderm (AVE) determines the A-P axis, yet the cues directing migration remain elusive. Here, we show that anisotropic compression directs AVE migration toward the minor-axis end of the deformed embryo, using ex utero culture with controlled compression and in utero pharmacological manipulations of uterine mechanics. This compression induces localized accumulation of basement membrane (BM) components, including COLLAGEN IV, which directs the AVE toward the minor-axis end. Mathematical modeling demonstrates that BM density-dependent AVE-BM adhesion accounts for the observed AVE dynamics. Our findings reveal that the maternal mechanical environment provides directional cues for cell migration, bridging tissue-scale mechanics and biochemical patterning during body axis specification.

items.title: Oligodendrocyte ER-phagy restricts excessive myelination by degrading sphingolipid synthases
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Molecular Biology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA.; Hamon Center for Regenerative Science and Medicine, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA.; Peter O’Donnell Jr. Brain Institute, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390, USA.
items.abstract: Myelination is critical for nervous system function. Numerous signaling pathways have been identified that promote myelin sheath growth, disruption of which can lead to hypomyelination. However, the negative regulators of myelin sheath expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we identify endoplasmic reticulum (ER)–phagy as a cellular brake on central nervous system myelination that restricts myelin sheath thickness during brain development. ER-phagy is active in oligodendrocytes during myelin membrane expansion and limits the abundance of ER-resident sphingolipid synthases, including ceramide synthase 2 (Cers2). Impairment of ER-phagy accumulates ER, elevates sphingolipid production, drives excessive myelin thickening, and alters social behavior after prolonged juvenile social isolation. Genetic deletion of Cers2, which synthesizes long-chain ceramides essential for sphingolipid biogenesis, rescues the hypermyelination phenotype caused by ER-phagy disruption. Together, our findings establish that ER-phagy–sphingolipid axis represses myelin growth and reveal a mechanistic link between ER homeostasis and myelin production by oligodendrocytes, providing insight into the cellular mechanisms underlying pathological hypermyelination.

Blood-Pressure–Lowering Treatment across the Cardiovascular Risk Spectrum
items.last_author_affiliation: Deep Medicine, Nuffield Department of Women’s and Reproductive Health, Medical Sciences Division, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom; Department of Cardiology, Imam Khomeini Hospital, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Tehran, Iran
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Treatment for lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of cardiovascular events among persons at high risk. Whether this benefit extends to those at lower risk remains unclear. METHODS: We performed a meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomized trials comparing antihypertensive treatment (intervention) with placebo, an active comparator, or usual care (comparator). The primary outcome was the first occurrence of a major cardiovascular event (fatal or nonfatal stroke, fatal or nonfatal ischemic heart disease, or heart failure resulting in death or hospitalization; composite outcome). Safety was assessed in trials that compared antihypertensive treatment with placebo or usual care, according to three prespecified composite outcomes: cardiovascular or hemodynamic events (palpitations, bradycardia, or hypotension), adverse renal events, and neurovestibular or fall-associated events. Participants were grouped into deciles according to predicted 5-year risk of a major cardiovascular event (median, 12.3%; lowest decile, <4%; highest decile, >27%). RESULTS: We included data from 51 trials and 357,440 participants - 169,042 in the intervention group and 188,398 in the comparator group. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, a major cardiovascular event occurred in 19,202 participants (11.4%) in the intervention group and in 24,398 (13.0%) in the comparator group. The overall estimated hazard ratio for a major cardiovascular event per 5-mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure was 0.90 (95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 0.92), with no evidence of variation across deciles. The absolute reduction in the 5-year cumulative risk of a major cardiovascular event was greater in the highest decile than in the lowest decile (2.6 vs. 0.4 percentage points), and the number needed to treat to prevent one major cardiovascular event over 5 years was lower in the highest decile than in the lowest decile (38 vs. 255). The incidence of a cardiovascular or hemodynamic event was 12.0 per 1000 person-years in the intervention group and 6.5 per 1000 person-years in the comparator group; the incidence of an adverse renal event was 3.3 and 2.2 per 1000 person-years, respectively; and the incidence of a neurovestibular or fall-associated event was 19.1 and 16.6 per 1000 person-years. The relative increase in the risk of each safety-outcome event with antihypertensive treatment as compared with placebo or usual care did not appear to vary across deciles. CONCLUSIONS: Blood-pressure lowering was associated with a decreased risk of major cardiovascular events across the risk spectrum, including a predicted 5-year risk below 4%. (Funded by the British Heart Foundation; PROSPERO registry number, CRD42018099283.).

items.title: Giant-Cell Arteritis
items.last_author_affiliation: Department of Rheumatology, Unidade Local de Saúde de Santa Maria, Centro Académico de Medicina de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal; Faculdade de Medicina, Universidade de Lisboa, Centro Académico de Medicina de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal
items.abstract: Giant-cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium-sized arteries that occurs almost exclusively in older adults. Suspected giant-cell arteritis warrants urgent diagnostic evaluation and, when ischemic risk is high, immediate treatment before diagnostic confirmation. Although glucocorticoids remain the cornerstone of therapy, treatment is frequently prolonged, associated with substantial toxic effects, and complicated by relapses. Advances in vascular imaging and insights into disease immunopathogenesis have expanded our understanding of disease heterogeneity and enabled the development of targeted therapies, particularly interleukin-6-receptor and Janus kinase inhibitors. Here, we review current concepts in the pathogenesis, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and management of giant-cell arteritis and highlight areas of uncertainty that warrant further investigation.

items.title: Epitope-conditioned generation of T-cell receptor β-chain CDR3 candidates using a pre-trained transformer model.
items.last_author_affiliation: AI for Life Sciences Lab, Tencent, Nanshan District, Shenzhen, 518054, China. jianhua.yao@gmail.com.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prioritizing T-cell receptor (TCR) candidates for defined peptide-HLA targets is an important step in TCR-based immunotherapy development, but it still relies heavily on laborious and expensive experimental screening. Recent advancements in generative artificial intelligence have demonstrated promising power in protein design and engineering. In this regard, we propose a pre-trained transformer model, termed Epitope-Receptor-Transformer (ERTransformer), for the epitope-conditioned generation of candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences. RESULTS: ERTransformer is built on EpitopeBERT and ReceptorBERT, which are trained using 1.9 million epitope sequences and 33.1 million TCR sequences, respectively. To demonstrate the model capability, we generate 1,000 candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences for each of the five epitopes with known natural TCRs. The generated candidates show low sequence similarity to natural TCR β-chains while retaining plausible CDR3 length, amino-acid composition, and conservative substitution patterns. We further conduct wet-lab experiments using flow cytometry in defined TCR/pMHC contexts and find that the level of T cell activation induced by selected artificial TCRs is either comparable to or even surpasses that of natural ones. CONCLUSIONS: Our work suggests that ERTransformer can expand and prioritize candidate TCR β-chain CDR3 sequences for downstream experimental screening in defined peptide-HLA and TCR-chain contexts.

items.title: Perplexity as a metric for isoform diversity in the human transcriptome.
items.last_author_affiliation: New York Genome Center, New York, NY, USA. daknowles@nygenome.org.; Department of Computer Science, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. daknowles@nygenome.org.; Department of Systems Biology, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. daknowles@nygenome.org.; Data Science Institute, Columbia University, New York, NY, USA. daknowles@nygenome.org.
items.abstract: Characterizing the extensive isoform diversity revealed by long-read RNA-sequencing remains challenging. After removal of technical artifacts, existing pipelines apply arbitrary expression thresholds that filter out bona fide transcript structures, obscuring diversity and hindering reproducibility. Instead of discarding isoforms, we propose a fundamentally distinct approach to quantifying isoform diversity using perplexity-the effective number of isoforms for a gene, derived from Shannon entropy-wherein every isoform, including low-abundance ones, contributes proportionally to a gene's diversity. Analyzing 124 ENCODE4 PacBio datasets spanning 55 human cell types, we show that perplexity provides interpretable and reproducible isoform diversity measurements across genes, regulatory levels, and tissues.

items.title: Organic matter composition modulates its degradation under the combined effects of iron (oxyhydr)oxides and light.
items.last_author_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Plateau Ecology and Agriculture, Qinghai University, Xining, PR China.
items.abstract: The extent of organic matter (OM) degradation in sunlit surface soils and shallow marine sediments is critical to global carbon and nitrogen cycling.
