items.title: Fixed-confidence identification of combination interventions in stochastic gene-network models, with a benchmark and an application to acute myeloid leukemia
items.corresponding_institution: Scientific Computing Programme, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
items.abstract: Mechanistic gene-network models are widely used to rank drug-target combinations. Each ranking rests on a finite number of noisy simulations, yet the confidence that the top-ranked set is truly best in the model is rarely stated. We formulate intervention search in a stochastic network model as fixed-confidence best-arm identification and give certified search: empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences that return an {varepsilon}-optimal intervention set with probability at least 1 - 2{delta} under any sampling rule, with successive elimination and batch-parallel LUCB as sampling rules. We compare them with uniform sampling, successive halving, greedy forward selection, sequential LUCB and UGapE, and ablate each design choice, on four networks (a BeatAML-calibrated AML network and three published cancer Boolean models; 1,275 to 5,488 candidate sets) under a protocol written before the runs. All 21 certified benchmark runs returned an {varepsilon}-optimal set (exact one-sided 95% lower bound 86.7%), as did all 4,560 and 1,980 replayed runs of the comparisons, using 6.4 to 19.0 times fewer simulations than uniform sampling with the same guarantee. Elimination and the variance-adaptive radius account for most of the saving (2.1 to 34.1 and 1.3 to 3.9 times). Sequential LUCB and UGapE use fewer simulations in total but are slow on parallel hardware; batch-parallel LUCB, with as many candidates per round as workers, was at most 1% slower than successive elimination in any setting and up to 3.2 times faster, and on the three published networks used 2.0 to 3.1 times fewer simulations. Applied to AML, a search over eight drug classes returns ibrutinib + midostaurin + an ERK-inhibitor class (model score 0.710 against 0.448 untreated), which is the best set in all 15 related calibrations of the network and exceeds additive and Bliss-independence expectations.

items.title: Human iPSC-derived Olfactory Sensory Organoids model olfactory function and drug response
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Engineering, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD 21218, USA; Department of Neurosurgery, Johns Hopkins Medical Institutes, Baltimor
items.abstract: Intranasal drug delivery is being explored as an alternative approach to overcome the blood-brain barrier in the treatment of central nervous system diseases. However, little is known about how therapeutics administered through this route affect human olfactory tissue. Here, we develop human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived olfactory sensory organoids that reproduce key cellular and functional features of the developing olfactory system. Over three months of differentiation, the organoids acquire diverse neuronal and glial-associated populations, including cells expressing markers of olfactory sensory neurons and interneurons. Single-nuclei RNA sequencing shows changes in cellular composition and lineage-associated transcriptional programs during maturation, while comparison with a human fetal nasal atlas identifies shared neural populations and developmental signatures. Alongside these molecular changes, the organoids develop spontaneous electrical activity and coordinated network bursting. Exposure to the glioma-relevant kinase inhibitors Dasatinib, Trametinib, and Selumetinib produces distinct changes in neuronal network activity, demonstrating the ability of the model to capture compound-associated functional responses. Together, these findings establish a human Olfactory Sensory Organoid system for investigating olfactory development and evaluating how therapeutics may affect olfactory neural tissue during intranasal drug administration.

items.title: A functional analysis of action potential generation in the axon initial segment in two autism mouse models with loss-of-function mutations of the Nav1.2 sodium channel
items.corresponding_institution: Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, LIPhy, F-38000 Grenoble, France
items.abstract: Loss-of-function (LoF) mutations of the SCN2A gene, coding for Nav1.2 Na+ channels, are among the leading genetic contributors to autism spectrum disorders and intellectual disability (ASD/ID). The haploinsufficient Scn2a knock-out mouse (Scn2a+/-), displaying ASD/ID-like phenotypes, is commonly used as model for this channelopathy, although this specific mutation has not been identified in patients. We investigated the action potential (AP) generation in the axon initial segment (AIS) of layer-5 neocortical pyramidal neurons in wild-type (Scn2a+/+) mice, in Scn2a+/- mice and in mice carrying the missense mutation L1314P (Scn2a+/L1314P), identified in an ASD/ID patient. We recorded somatic action potentials (APs), and imaged Na+, Ca2+ and APs in the AIS, in females during postnatal (P) P21-40. During maturation from P21-24 to P30-40: (1) the ratio between Na+ influx in proximal and distal AIS sites (Rp/d) increased; (2) the delay between distal and proximal Ca2+ currents increased; (3) the half-width of the AP (APwid) in the soma decreased. We revealed that this maturation process is different in both Scn2a+/- and Scn2a+/L1314P mice, but in divergent manner. With respect to Scn2a+/+, Scn2a+/- cells were characterised by smaller Rp/d and delay values at P30-40, and wider somatic APwid at P21-24, whereas Scn2a+/L1314P cells by shorter AIS APwid at P21-24. Using a biophysical model, mimicking maturation changes in terms of Nav1.2, of a K+ channel and of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, we reproduced the ensemble of experimental results, establishing that Scn2a+/- cells exhibit a combination of Nav1.2 LoF and delayed development, whereas Scn2a+/L1314P cells are characterised by AIS disruption involving strongly increased functional K+ channels. We conclude that diverse Nav1.2 LoF cases lead to different developmental paths involving other channels.

items.title: Frequency-Selective Responses to Temporal Interference Stimulation in Hippocampal Neurons
items.abstract: Temporal interference (TI) stimulation aims to engage deep brain structures noninvasively by superimposing two slightly detuned high-frequency electric fields (e.g. > 2 kHz), producing a low-frequency envelope (1-120 Hz) where they overlap. Existing accounts explain why a neuron responds to the envelope, but none identifies what determines which beat frequency a given neuron amplifies most. We address this using morphologically detailed, conductance-based models of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons and four interneuron subtypes, varying carrier frequency, envelope frequency, field amplitude, and orientation. Since the applied field contains no spectral component at the beat frequency, that response must first be generated by nonlinear membrane dynamics; we characterize the frequency-dependent gain applied to it once generated. That gain is band-pass: slow voltage-gated currents suppress the response at low frequencies and produce a peak at the resonant frequency. Modulated stimulation therefore outperforms an unmodulated carrier only when the envelope frequency matches the resonance of the relevant compartment, near its firing threshold. Notably, this advantage extends to carriers as low as 250 Hz, well below the minimum reported for simplified neuron models (1400-1700 Hz). Under distributed synaptic drive the advantage is lost, although frequency selectivity persists. Selectivity also varies across targets: because resonance depends on conductance composition, the optimal envelope frequency differs across compartments and cell types, and augmenting resonant conductances in parvalbumin-positive basket cells confers an advantage they otherwise lack. Carrier frequency is therefore less constrained than commonly assumed, and envelope frequency should be matched to the resonant properties of the target neuron type.

items.title: Developmental timeline of the lateral olfactory tract innervation of piriform cortex
items.abstract: The development of the lateral olfactory tract (LOT) begins embryonically and is closely linked to the differentiation of olfactory bulb (OB) projection neurons, mitral and tufted cells, whose axons form the LOT. Here, we implemented calretinin (CR) as a proxy to characterize LOT development. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) for CR revealed expression in most mitral/tufted cells, with lower levels in the dorsal OB. This mirrored a reduced CR labeling in a restricted ventral LOT domain, suggesting topographic organization of OB projections. To achieve axonal resolution, we used Calb2-CreERT2 x Ai14 mice to label CR+ neurons and their axons with tdTomato. Expression began at E12, when pioneer LOT axons reach the anterior piriform cortex (APC) and posterior brain regions. From E13-E14, axon density increased, contributing to LOT thickening and extension toward the amygdala. Axonal arborization was not evident in the posterior piriform cortex (PPC) until E15. Electron microscopy revealed excitatory asymmetric and inhibitory symmetric synapses in the APC as early as E13, with relatively stable embryonic densities. Postnatally, excitatory synapses increased in both APC and PPC between P9 and P21. Collectively, this work establishes a developmental timeline of LOT formation and sheds light on fundamental aspects of the assembly of olfactory cortical circuits.

items.title: Functional and Neurotransmitter Organization of Cortical Gray Matter Remodeling During Pregnancy
items.abstract: Pregnancy is a period of profound neuroplasticity, marked by widespread, spatially heterogeneous reductions in cortical gray matter volume (GMV). Yet, whether this remodeling affects cognition is unclear: subjective memory complaints are common during pregnancy, but objective findings are mixed. Using densely sampled longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) across pregnancy, we examined whether gestational GMV change corresponds spatially with normative maps of cognitive function and neurotransmitter receptors. We analyzed 19 T1-weighted MRI sessions of 1 healthy primiparous woman spanning preconception to 36 weeks gestational age. The GMV change map was annotated using 10 cognitive domain maps comprised of 115 Neurosynth terms and 16 positron emission tomography receptor and transporter maps from healthy adults, using dominance analysis and partial least squares (PLS) analysis with spin tests to account for spatial autocorrelation. Total cortical GMV declined by 4.24%. The 10 cognitive domains accounted for significant spatial variation in GMV change (R2adj = 0.16; spin P = .03), with learning and memory (37.7%) and action (27.3%) accounting for the largest shares of explained variance. PLS revealed a shared spatial axis in which learning and memory were associated with smaller GMV reductions while action was associated with greater reductions (spin P = .046). The receptor and transporter maps also accounted for significant spatial variation (R2adj = 0.22; spin P = .02). PLS identified a significant neurochemical pattern (spin P = .009), with greater GMV reductions in regions rich in cholinergic (VAChT) and noradrenergic (NET) markers and smaller reductions in regions rich in serotonergic, GABAA, and muscarinic M1 receptors. This receptor-derived pattern was positively associated with social function and negatively associated with action. Together, these findings provide new evidence that pregnancy-related GMV remodeling is organized along functional and neurotransmitter receptor axes, suggesting that maternal brain plasticity is a targeted process that may support selective cognitive adaptation.

items.title: Separating robust from fragile cell-type changes in spatial transcriptomics using screening label uncertainty to identify composition effects
items.abstract: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics platforms such as 10x Xenium measure thousands of genes in intact tissue at single-cell resolution, making them attractive for screening which cell populations change between experimental conditions. In small studies, however, apparent changes in cell-type composition can arise from misannotated cells rather than biology, and the reliability of individual cell-type calls is rarely reported. We present SLUICE (Screening Label Uncertainty to Identify Composition Effects), an R/Seurat workflow that classifies each cell by atlas-informed marker scoring and records a per-cell confidence margin and runner-up identity. Each group difference is then tested against three diagnostics: region-specific confidence thresholds, sensitivity analyses that reassign borderline calls, and single-gene driver checks that combine gene co-detection, runner-up identity, and spatial location. Applied to Xenium Prime 5K data from six mice (three traumatic brain injury, three sham) in two contrasting regions, the hippocampus and the optic tract, confidence thresholds differed almost sevenfold between regions (0.17 vs 0.026), showing that a fixed cutoff does not transfer between tissues. Driver checks identified mislabelled populations that margin-based filtering left in place, including Klotho (Kl)-expressing neurons called choroid plexus in the hippocampus and Csf3r-expressing myeloid cells called neutrophils in the optic tract. Excluding the neutrophil panel reduced the number of optic tract categories whose group difference changed direction from five to two (one of which was the Unclassified category), while the major glial populations were stable across all analyses. SLUICE separates robust from fragile composition changes, identifying which shifts merit experimental follow-up before time and tissue are committed to them. Code is available at https://github.com/rebeccasakko/hippocampus-xenium-analysis.

items.title: Mapping the invisible: Incidental spatial encoding through haptic exploration
items.abstract: Active touch provides rich spatial information about object shape. Whether this haptic information can be retained without an explicit memorisation goal remains unclear. Participants explored an unfamiliar two-dimensional raised-dot contour under different sensory conditions and memorisation instructions. Two haptic groups traced the contour hidden from view, either without advance knowledge of the memory tasks (Haptic-Naive) or with explicit memorisation instructions (Haptic-Informed). Reference groups traced the visible contour (Visuo-Haptic-Naive) or viewed it without tracing (Visual-Naive), both without memorisation instructions. Retention was assessed through manual shape reproduction and visual recognition, with a Random-Control group drawing arbitrary shapes as a reproduction baseline. Reproductions in all exploration groups were more similar to the target than arbitrary drawings, supporting incidental spatial encoding in the Haptic-Naive group. Memorisation instructions produced no detectable reproduction advantage but altered exploratory behaviour. Visual feedback improved online tracing without a detectable reproduction advantage over haptic-only exploration. Visual-Naive participants reproduced the shape more accurately than Haptic-Naive participants. Recognition scores were higher following memorisation instructions or exploration with visual information, although Haptic-Naive participants selected alternatives relatively similar to the target. Source-space EEG analyses in the Haptic-Naive group revealed widespread beta-power reductions across bilateral somatosensory, parietal, and occipital regions. Greater reductions in the left lateral occipital complex were associated with more accurate subsequent reproduction. Together, these findings indicate that active touch can support incidental spatial encoding and is associated with changes in cortical activity. The accessibility and use of the retained information are shaped by the goals and sensory context of exploration.

items.title: Modelling mouse barrel cortex: from anatomical structure to cortical dynamics
items.abstract: Detailed biophysical simulations of neuronal networks might help understand brain function. Here, we built a model of mouse barrel cortex focused on its somatotopic map, comprising 33 barrel columns. We investigated dendritic polarity in layer 4 and implemented it in the model, building two circuits differing in a single property of basal dendritic synthesis. In the polarised circuit, layer 4 dendrites were confined to their home barrel; in the symmetric circuit, they were not. We simulated three conditions: i) quiet periods without whisker movement; ii) active free-whisking periods without touch; and iii) active whisking with touch of the C2 whisker. The model exhibited complex spatiotemporal dynamics of neuronal activity across cortical layers, cortical columns, molecularly-defined classes of neurons, and brain states. Using cyclicity analysis, spiking responses were decomposed into activity shared between the two circuits and activity unique to either. Layer 4 dendritic polarisation sharpened the touch response in space and advanced it in time.

items.title: Sex differences in corticostriatal regulation of alcohol drinking following chronic intermittent alcohol exposure
items.abstract: Background: Sex differences in alcohol use disorder (AUD) suggest that the neural circuits regulating alcohol intake may differ between males and females. We examined whether infralimbic neurons projecting to the nucleus accumbens shell (IL-NAcSh) regulate alcohol self-administration and anxiety-related behavior following chronic intermittent alcohol (CIA) exposure. Methods: Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats were trained to self-administer 10% alcohol before receiving excitatory, inhibitory or control designer receptors exclusively activated by designer drugs (DREADDs) in NAcSh-projecting IL neurons. Rats then underwent six weeks of CIA vapor or room air exposure. Alcohol self-administration and elevated plus maze behavior was then assessed after deschloroclozapine pretreatment. Results: During acute withdrawal, IL-NAcSh inhibition increased alcohol intake in CIA-exposed males, while excitation increased intake in room air control males. Neither manipulation detectably altered alcohol intake in females. In the elevated plus maze, excitation reduced open-arm time and increased closed-arm time in males, while both excitation and inhibition reduced open-arm time in females. Conclusions: Activity in NAcSh-projecting IL neurons appears to constrain alcohol intake during acute withdrawal in CIA-exposed males. Increasing activity in these neurons did not reduce intake in this group. The divergent effects on EPM behavior and drinking suggest that this pathway's contributions to anxiety-like behavior and alcohol self-administration are partly dissociable. The absence of detectable effects on drinking in females highlights the need to identify additional pathways that regulate dependence-related alcohol use in females. Better defining the circuits that regulate withdrawal-induced drinking in males and females may guide the development of more effective, sex-informed circuit-based therapies for AUD.

items.title: Supplier-associated variation in motor performance and cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neuron anatomy in C57BL/6 mice
items.abstract: Cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons (CSF-cNs) are an evolutionarily conserved population of spinal sensory neurons positioned around the central canal and characterized by expression of the ion channel PKD2L1. CSF-cNs contribute to locomotor control, but little is known about variation in this sensory system among commonly used laboratory mouse populations. We compared motor performance and CSF-cN organization in closely related C57BL/6 mice obtained from The Jackson Laboratory (Jackson), Charles River Laboratories (Charles River), and Taconic Biosciences (Taconic). Motor performance differed among suppliers, with Charles River mice performing better than Taconic mice on balance beam and rotarod tasks, whereas grid walking performance did not differ significantly among groups. CSF-cN organization also differed significantly among suppliers. Jackson mice had the greatest abundance of PKD2L1+ cells and canal-contacting cells, and a greater proportion of PKD2L1+ cells contacted the central canal in Jackson mice than in Charles River or Taconic mice. CSF-cNs were also more abundant in cervical than lumbar spinal cord regions, whereas the proportion contacting the canal showed only a trend toward a regional difference. Individual CSF-cN measures did not show significant associations with motor performance. These findings demonstrate significant supplier-associated variation in both motor performance and the organization of the CSF-cN anatomy and show that greater CSF-cN abundance does not necessarily correspond to better motor performance.

items.title: Severity of Addiction-like Behaviors and Sex Distinctly Promote Oxycodone-Related Behaviors in Heterogeneous Stock Rats
items.abstract: The opioid epidemic continues to impose substantial public health burdens. Critical gaps remain in understanding how sex and individual differences contribute to opioid addiction-like behavior. Although previous clinical and preclinical work has identified sex and other individual differences in opioid-related outcomes, it remains unclear whether the magnitude of sex differences varies across behavioral domains and levels of individual addiction-like vulnerability. To address this gap, we analyzed data from 810 genetically diverse heterogeneous stock (HS) rats that underwent oxycodone self-administration under short-access (2h/day) and extended-access (12h/day) conditions. Addiction-like behavior was characterized across four domains comprising escalation of oxycodone intake, motivation to obtain oxycodone, tolerance to oxycodone-induced analgesia, and withdrawal-induced hyperalgesia. These measures were integrated into a composite Addiction Index (AI) to characterize individual addiction-like severity, with animals classified into four groups: resilient, mild, moderate, and severe. Sex differences were then examined across behavioral outcomes, AI groups, and experimental cohorts. Estrous-phase effects on motivation, relationships among behavioral dimensions, and within-session patterns of oxycodone intake were also examined. Females exhibited greater oxycodone intake and motivation than males following extended access, whereas pain-related behavioral outcomes showed greater associations across levels of addiction-like severity than between sexes. Although sex differences were observed for specific behavioral outcomes, further analyses provided no evidence that their magnitude varied across AI groups. Estrous phase did not significantly affect motivation for oxycodone. Pooled sex effects supported greater self-administration and motivation in females, whereas pooled sex effects for pain-related outcomes were not significant and showed varying degrees of between-cohort heterogeneity. Temporal features of oxycodone intake also differed by sex and were associated with addiction-like severity, with titration-phase intake showing the strongest association with the AI. Relationships among addiction-related behavioral dimensions were largely similar between females and males, although specific associations differed by sex and across AI groups. These findings demonstrate that sex and individual variability contribute in different ways to oxycodone addiction-like behavior. Female-biased differences were most apparent following extended access, whereas pain-related behavioral outcomes showed greater associations across levels of addiction-like severity. Together, these results highlight the importance of multidimensional phenotyping for characterizing sex and individual variability in opioid addiction-like behavior. Keywords: sex differences; individual differences, Heterogeneous Stock rats; estrous cycle; oxycodone; opioids; addiction-like behavior

items.title: Linking Molecular Changes in the Hypothalamus to Alzheimer's Disease Phenotypes
items.abstract: In many individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD), sleep disruption and weight loss emerge years before the onset of memory decline and dementia. However, the cellular and molecular bases of these early events are not well understood. The hypothalamus is a critical brain region for the regulation of these behaviors, but its response to amyloid has not been systematically characterized. We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing to generate transcriptomic profiles of 1.1 million nuclei across the hypothalamus from 10 genetic backgrounds of the AD-BXD genetic reference panel spanning two ages and both sexes, including age-matched controls. Amyloid was associated with widespread, sex-biased molecular changes across diverse cell classes, including elevated neuroinflammatory signatures in microglia and astrocytes, upregulated ion transport pathways across barrier-associated cell types, and sex- and age-dependent changes to primary ciliary pathways in Glp1r+/Lepr+, Histaminergic, and Hcrt+ neuronal populations. Two metabolism-related populations showed differential expression exclusively in one sex: Glp1r+/Lepr+ neurons in females and Gpr50+ neurons in males. Several findings were conserved in analysis of human hypothalamus snRNAseq data, including reduced expression of TGF-{beta} pathway genes in medial mammillary body neurons and increased relative abundance of reactive Serpina3n+/YKL-40 astrocytes. This atlas provides a cellular framework for understanding the early, non-cognitive symptoms of AD and identifies several hypothalamic cell-type specific pathways that represent potential targets for therapeutic intervention.

items.title: How Experience Becomes a Program: Episodic Memory as a Difference Engine
items.abstract: A child who has seen a few sums can add numbers of any length: finite experience has become a program, a procedure with memory that holds for inputs of every size. Networks learn procedures by passing errors backward through every step of a computation, over many examples, and what they learn on short inputs seldom holds on long ones. Brains keep something networks discard, the experiences themselves, and we propose that they keep them in order to compare them. When two remembered experiences differ in one place, the first answer at which they differ depended on that place. This method of difference finds the cause of an answer in one step, however long the computation in between, and finds causes that act jointly, each of which alone is invisible to statistics. We show that such comparisons write programs. Comparing an experience with one that differs in a single symbol shows what each answer depends on; in a memory that recalls the past by counting events, each dependence is a linear equation, and the stack, the queue and the counter of computer science are solutions of such equations. Comparing what follows two beginnings shows which states a program must keep, and comparing a question with the question one symbol shorter builds each answer from the one before. Where experience does not decide, nothing is guessed: the learner asks, or says that it does not know. A machine built on these principles, with no backpropagation and no search over programs, writes exact programs for thirteen of the fifteen tasks of a standard benchmark, each in under a minute, from a few hundred short strings and, for two of the tasks, questions of its own; eleven of the programs hold at a million symbols. It learns tasks withheld from its design, builds multiplication from its own addition, and in 5,680 runs announces no false program. The hippocampus has the form of such a difference engine: it stores whole episodes after one exposure, keeps similar ones apart, recalls a neighbour of the present and compares the two. In simulated circuits of neurons the programs run exactly, a replayed sweep finds where two episodes differ, and a local rule learns the gains with no backward pass. On this account, episodic memory is the brain's means of assigning credit by comparison.

items.title: Brain pericyte lineages converge on a shared molecular profile
items.abstract: Brain pericytes arise from two embryonic lineages, neural crest and mesoderm, but it is unknown whether these origins produce molecularly distinct pericyte populations. Using zebrafish lineage-tracing transgenics, we mapped neural crest- and mesoderm-derived pericytes across the brain from larval to adult stages. Neural crest-derived pericytes occupied the forebrain and mesoderm-derived pericytes occupied the midbrain and hindbrain at early stages. A population of neural crest-derived pericytes then appeared in the dorsal midbrain by 10 days post-fertilization and persisted into adulthood. A small population of mesoderm-derived pericytes also appeared in the ventral forebrain of juvenile and adult fish. Bulk RNA sequencing of FACS-isolated adult pericytes showed that the two lineages share expression of canonical pericyte genes, with only 30 genes differentially expressed. Fluorescent in situ hybridization validated one neural crest-enriched gene, plpp3, and several mesoderm-enriched genes, including loxl2b. Together, these data suggest that despite distinct embryonic origins and regional bias, brain pericyte lineages converge on a largely shared molecular profile.

items.title: Methods for precise targeting and modulation of the axon initial segment
items.corresponding_institution: Southern University of Science and Technology
items.abstract: The axon initial segment (AIS) is fundamental to action potential initiation, neuronal polarity maintenance, and plasticity. Despite its functional importance, AIS remains understudied partially due to the lack of molecular tools with high subcellular specificity. By engineering an ultra-high affinity (Kd ~0.37 nM) small binder (16 kDa) that exclusively targets 480-kDa ankyrin-G, the master scaffold of AIS, and integrating neuronal type-specific promoters with feedback-regulated expression elements, we developed an efficient, portable method for delivering tightly controlled amounts of proteins or organelles to the AIS with unprecedented specificity, enabling selective, tunable, and near-endogenous-level AIS targeting in defined neuronal populations both in vitro and in vivo. Coupled with a toolkit of AIS modulators that we characterized, this strategy achieves directed manipulation of AIS structure, real-time monitoring of AIS plasticity dynamics and fast degradation of the entire AIS compartment, in desired neuronal types. Thus, our method provides new opportunities for dissecting AIS physiology and pathology, facilitating the development of therapeutics for AIS-linked brain disorders.

items.title: Multicellular nodules form at subacute time points following closed-head diffuse traumatic brain injury in pigs
items.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of long-term neurological impairments and is associated with persistent neuroinflammation. Multicellular nodules, composed of densely aggregated myeloid cells, have been reported in human post-mortem tissue following TBI but remain poorly characterized. Here, we utilized a clinically relevant porcine model of closed-head diffuse TBI generated through rotational acceleration to characterize the temporal and spatial distribution of these nodules. Nodules were rare in sham animals and minimally present at acute time points but increased significantly by 14 days post injury. Nodule burden increased as a function of injury severity and was positively correlated with rotational injury velocity. Nodules were enriched within white matter structures, including subcortical white matter, corpus callosum, fornix, and internal capsule, while remaining minimally present in cortical gray matter. Within these regions, nodules exhibited a widespread yet spatially organized distribution rather than local clustering around a single anatomical location. Together, these findings demonstrate that multicellular nodules are a robust and reproducible neuroinflammatory pathology following diffuse TBI in a gyrencephalic large-animal model. By establishing the temporal progression, severity dependence, and white matter enrichment of this clinically relevant but understudied endophenotype, this work provides a foundation for future investigations into the mechanisms and consequences of post-traumatic neuroinflammation.

items.title: Neurogenic archetypes and diversifiers configure the molecular and functional organization of corticofugal output channels
items.abstract: Cortical extratelencephalic neurons (ET) derive from either direct neurogenesis from radial glia cells (ETd) or indirect neurogenesis through intermediate progenitors (ETi), but whether and how neurogenic origin contributes to ET diversity and function remains unknown. Using genetic strategies that differentially target ETd and ETi, we profiled their transcriptomes across the isocortex and imaged their activity in motor cortex during a reach-grasp-drink (RGD) task. While both ETd and ETi contribute to all transcriptomically-defined ET subtypes, they diverge significantly in the concerted expression profile of effector-gene families that shape transcriptional regulation, neuronal connectivity and physiology. During the RGD task, motor cortex ETd formed a small yet heterogeneous pool of broadly tuned activity archetypes, while ETi included a diversified set of spatially organized subpopulations that tracked successive actions of RGD. Therefore, neurogenic origin defines a developmental axis of neuronal diversification orthogonal to the current transcriptomic classification scheme, in which ETi differ from ETd transcriptomically through coordinated significant shifts in effector-gene families, while functionally in the motor cortex, they elaborate a small pool of task-generic ETd into specialized output channels that track different phases of goal-directed RGD behavior.

items.title: Reciprocal 16p11.2 Copy Number Variants Differentially Alter Regional Brain Anatomy and Allometric Scaling
items.abstract: Reciprocal 16p11.2 copy-number variants (CNVs) confer substantial risk for neuropsychiatric disorders and produce opposing effects on brain size, with larger brain volume in deletion carriers and smaller volume in duplication carriers. Regional alterations broadly parallel this global phenotype, but because regional brain measures scale nonlinearly with brain size, it remains unclear whether regional differences reflect expected consequences of altered brain size, regional anatomy disproportionate to brain size, or fundamental alterations in allometric scaling. We analyzed 285 imaging sessions from 235 participants (49 deletion, 59 duplications, 127 controls) using log-log allometric models to distinguish these possibilities. Brain-size adjustment revealed widespread cortical disproportion in both CNVs, with predominantly reciprocal effects driven by surface area rather than cortical thickness, whereas subcortical structures showed convergent reductions disproportionate to brain size. Strikingly, examining genotype-specific scaling exponents revealed distinct allometric patterns between the CNVs. In duplication, regional differences predominantly reflected fixed shifts relative to brain size. In deletion, by contrast, regional differences more frequently varied with brain size, with substantial exponent deviations affecting 32% of disproportionate cortical regions compared with 12% in duplication. Thus, reciprocal 16p11.2 dosage does not simply shift regional anatomy in opposite directions: duplication largely preserves the normally conserved scaling of regional anatomy with brain size, whereas deletion more extensively disrupts it.

items.title: An Open, Evolving Brain and Cognitive Aging Simulator Enabled by Agentic Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: An agentic AI simulator was built to advance our understanding about how the human brain and cognition change with age. The simulator generates worlds based on hypothesized age-linked cascades and then simulates studies across varied experimental designs and selection criteria. Each simulated world begins with 120,000 individual lives initiated by baseline parameters (e.g., genetic risk, birth year) and then changed by age-dependent cascades (e.g., amyloid-dependent, cardiovascular). Examples illustrate how the simulator predicts distinct data patterns in cross-sectional versus longitudinal designs, how alternative participant selection strategies emphasize baseline differences versus age-related decline, and how variable levels of association emerge between brain and cognition dependent upon design choices. Simulations of clinical trials provide information about design, power, and outcome considerations. Experiments on alternative simulated worlds evaluate how well hypothesized cascades accommodate real-world data patterns, capturing the insights and open puzzles inside the application. Most critically, the application is built to evolve. Its code contains a complete description of how to construct and update itself so that any person or AI agent can explore a new finding, recalibrate to emerging data, or build and simulate a novel future study. The simulator is offered as a tool for understanding data patterns, teaching, and generation of hypotheses to be tested in future studies using real-world data collection.

items.title: Neuronal communication subspaces arise across prefrontal-striatal circuits prior to gaze-directed object selection and develop with learning
items.abstract: How neuronal ensembles determine the most relevant object to attend to remains unresolved but likely involves coordinating information across multiple brain areas. We found support for this hypothesis in latent firing co-variations across the prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and head of the caudate (CD) during and after attention-set learning. Before gaze shifted to an object, neuronal communication subspaces emerged across area pairs. While exploring options during learning, ACC and PFC led communication over the CD prior to gaze shifts, which switched to the CD and PFC leading the ACC when exploiting learned attention sets. Neurons participating in exploration- and exploitation-specific subspaces were partly segregated and carried information about the value and location of the to-be-selected objects, suggesting they guide attention and gaze.

items.title: Excitation/Inhibition Balance in People at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis: A Functional MRI Study
items.abstract: Excitation/inhibition (E/I) imbalance is implicated in the pathophysiology of psychosis, but the extent to which this is evident before the onset of illness is unclear. Here, we investigated E/I-related brain dynamics using the Hurst exponent (HE) derived from resting-state MRI in two longitudinal cohorts of individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis (CHR-P): PSYSCAN (190 CHR-P individuals and 115 controls) and Accelerating Medicines Partnership(R) Schizophrenia (826 CHR-P individuals and 241 controls). Both cohorts showed lower whole-brain HE in CHR-P individuals than in controls at baseline, with the most prominent differences observed in the somatomotor network and thalamus. In both cohorts, normative receptor distributions significantly predicted the spatial pattern of HE differences, with consistent contributions from norepinephrine, serotonin, and opioid receptors. In PSYSCAN, 21 CHR-P individuals transitioned to psychosis during follow-up. There was preliminary evidence that subsequent transition to psychosis was associated with a longitudinal reduction in HE in the right inferior parietal cortex and that baseline regional HE showed above-chance prediction of subsequent transition at the individual level. Together, these findings suggest that vulnerability to psychosis is associated with reduced HE, consistent with less persistent brain dynamics and increased excitability.

items.title: The computational cost of explicit strategies in force-field adaptation
items.abstract: Sensorimotor adaptation is often attributed to an implicit, cerebellar-based process, particularly when learning to compensate for novel limb dynamics. However, recent evidence suggests that explicit strategies can also contribute to force-field adaptation, although how these strategies are represented and implemented is unclear. In visuomotor adaptation, explicit strategies can rely on an algorithmic-like process in which the time required to prepare a movement increases with the magnitude of the required correction. Here, we asked whether explicit compensation for force-field perturbations is generated through a similarly time-consuming computation. Human participants performed reaching movements in a paired-trial paradigm in which the force experienced on one movement could be used to prepare a counteracting response on the subsequent movement. Across two experiments, we found that when participants were encouraged to attempt to counteract the forces, movement preparation time increased systematically with force magnitude: larger compensatory responses required longer preparation. This relationship was substantially reduced when participants performed exactly the same task but were not informed about the paired-trial design, performance was significantly worse and was not accompanied by a corresponding increase in preparation time. These findings suggest that when participants use a strategy to improve performance in response to perturbing forces, it appears to be accomplished with a parametric, algorithmic-like process, one may be similar to strategies employed in visuomotor adaptation.

items.title: Mouse pup ultrasonic vocalization repertoires shift with age and behavioral context across the first postnatal week
items.abstract: Pup ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) are thought to communicate and elicit maternal care, yet the structure of the pup call repertoire and how it changes across the vulnerable first postnatal week remain poorly characterized. Here we analyzed approximately 59,000 USVs emitted by wildtype mouse pups (postnatal days P0-P5) during a pup retrieval paradigm that included habituation, pup isolation, and retrieval phases, performed with wild-type (WT) and Mecp2-heterozygous (Het) female mice as alloparental surrogates. Using DeepSqueak-based acoustic feature extraction and unsupervised clustering, we identified eight distinct call types, grouped into two broad classes based on shared acoustic properties. The relative prevalence and sequencing of these call types shifted systematically with postnatal age and behavioral phase, indicating that the pup vocal repertoire is both developmentally and contextually dynamic during the first postnatal week. However, call-type composition and acoustic characteristics did not differ with behavioral outcome, consistent with the model in which USVs function as general arousal signals integrated with other sensory cues. A candidate sequence-level pattern distinguished failed retrievals but was based on few calls and requires further validation. Pup call repertoire and developmental trajectory were also indistinguishable between WT and Het surrogates, indicating that the previously reported retrieval deficit in Het females does not arise from atypical pup vocal signals. Together, these results provide a detailed developmental and contextual map of the early pup call repertoire and a framework for relating call-type dynamics to auditory circuit plasticity across early postnatal life.

items.title: A Platform for Semi-automatic Segmentation, CharacteristicShape Analysis and Simulation of Neuronal Nuclei
items.abstract: Segmenting neuronal somas in 3D brain images obtained through techniques such as tissue clearing and Light Sheet Fluorescence Microscopy promises to advance our understanding of healthy brains and the pathophysiological roots of neurological diseases. However, manual segmentation methods are often costly and time-consuming. Automating the segmentation through deep neural networks shows promise, but requires labeled ground-truth data that is also labor-intensive and expensive to obtain. To address these limitations, this work provides a platform within the open-source 3D image analysis software Vaa3D to efficiently and precisely label and automatically segment neuronal somas. A binary image of segmented somas is generated using a region-growing algorithm applied on 3D somas marked and bounded by a sphere around their center of mass, guided by a local Otsu threshold that can be manually overridden. The platform further supports principal component analysis of the segmented somas, allowing them to be rotated about their center of mass and aligned, in order for their characteristic shape to be captured in a probabilistic model. Finally, the platform supports the simulation of soma segmentation: it probabilistically reorients, repositions, and deforms segmented somas obtained from real data, generating synthetic ground truth data that can be used to train deep neural networks.

items.title: Joint Representation of Valence and Arousal in the Human Brain
items.abstract: Scenes varying in emotional content are commonly characterized along two affective dimensions: hedonic valence, reflecting pleasantness, and emotional arousal, reflecting intensity. Although prior studies have examined neural representations of valence and arousal separately, it remains unclear how these dimensions are represented jointly and how their representation relates to low-level visual and scene-level properties. Here, we used representational similarity analysis (RSA) to identify brain regions whose activity patterns represented the joint valence-arousal structure of affective images and to compare this representation with those of low-level visual and scene-level properties. Twenty participants viewed 60 International Affective Picture System (IAPS) images during simultaneous EEG-fMRI recording. We constructed three image-level representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs): an Emotion RDM derived from valence and arousal ratings; a GIST RDM derived from low-level visual features captured by GIST descriptors; and a Scene RDM derived from CLIP-ViT image embeddings. Searchlight fMRI RSA identified joint valence-arousal representations in lateral occipitotemporal cortex, low-level visual representations in visual cortex, with smaller extensions into right STS and right insula, and scene-level representations across distributed occipital, temporal, parietal, and frontal regions. The valence-arousal representation showed little spatial overlap with the low-level visual representation but was spatially nested within regions representing scene-level properties. EEG-fMRI fusion further indicated that low-level visual representations emerged at approximately 124 ms after stimulus onset, followed by scene-level and valence-arousal representations at approximately 428 ms and 532 ms, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that joint valence-arousal representations are linked to higher-order scene representations, are distinct from low-level visual representations in both space and time, and may support the affective-semantic characterization of visual scenes. Exploratory analyses further showed that valence and arousal ratings generated by multimodal large language models (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini) corresponded closely with human ratings and yielded neural representation maps that substantially overlapped with the human valence-arousal map.

items.title: Benchmarking machine learning across development reveals stage-specific neuroanatomical sex signatures.
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) offers powerful approaches for identifying multivariate patterns in neuroimaging data, yet the biological validity and interpretability of the discriminative patterns learned by such models remain incompletely understood. Here, we benchmarked multiple ML approaches for sex classification across development (8-21 years) on structural neuroimaging data and investigated the effects of age on model performance and feature stability. Linear and nonlinear models demonstrated comparable classification performance, indicating that high predictive accuracy can be achieved without relying on highly complex architectures; however, age-stratified analyses and cross-age generalization tests demonstrated that developmental stage influences classification performance, and consistency of learned neuroanatomical features. To assess biological interpretability, we applied SHAP and LIME explainability methods and developed a comprehensive framework for translating feature attributions into biologically interpretable patterns. Sex-discriminative regions were distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical structures and exhibited marked developmental variation. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of interpretable ML for developmental neuroimaging and highlight the importance of evaluating predictive performance while simultaneously taking biological validity, developmental specificity, and attribution stability into consideration.

items.title: Sampling the Training Trajectory of Vision Models Reveals a Mismatch with Human Visual Development
items.abstract: We compare time-resolved EEG representational geometry across seven age groups, from 6 months to adulthood, with representations sampled throughout training from supervised and self-supervised ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16. Previous model-brain comparisons mostly used adult brain recordings and untrained or fully trained networks. We find that successive training stages do not systematically progress from child- to adult-like neural representations: alignment with every age group from 4 years onward emerges early in training and remains stable. Training adds substantial alignment beyond the untrained architecture, similarly at every age. Finally, categorical structure and spatial frequency each explain a stable share of the neural geometry at every age, with apparent age-related increases in categorical organization reflecting increased EEG reliability. Because standard training on full-resolution images aligns with all ages early, and spatial frequency, which depends on maturing visual acuity, strongly shapes the neural geometry, developmentally structured visual input may help models follow human visual development.

items.title: Does Denoising Reduce Cross-Vendor Variability in Diffusion MRI? A Travelling Heads Evaluation
items.abstract: Between-scanner variability in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived features can be comparable to biological between-subject variability, even for the same individual scanned at different sites. MRI harmonisation is therefore an essential tool to ensure studies are generalisable across sites, reducing between-scanner variability and enabling pooling of data to achieve large sample sizes and more representative population samples. Denoising using MPPCA is widely used in preprocessing pipelines for diffusion MRI acquisitions to improve image SNR and it has been proposed as an implicit way of harmonising data. In this registered report, we hypothesised that denoising reduces cross-scanner variability and improves reliability in diffusion MRI metrics without changing cross-scanner bias, and that susceptibility-induced off-resonance reduces its efficacy. We tested these hypotheses using a travelling-heads resource of ten subjects scanned on six scanners from three vendors (GE, Philips, Siemens), with within-scanner repeats. We found that: i) Denoising reduced voxel-wise cross-scanner coefficients of variation for fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) and mean kurtosis (MK) (BF > 100; median -3%, -9% and -32%). ROI-wise, variability decreased for MK (-12%), increased for FA (+8%), and evidence was inconclusive for MD. ii) Contrary to our hypothesis, denoising changed cross-scanner bias in every subject-scanner pair, by up to 3% of the mean; in exploratory analyses, this change was strongly related to contrast-to-noise ratio. iii) Evidence for a change in the registered measure of reliability was inconclusive, although exploratory analyses showed higher voxel-wise reliability after denoising. iv) There was no convincing evidence that off-resonance reduces denoising efficacy. Together, these results suggest that MPPCA denoising reduces the random, noise-driven component of cross-scanner variability, most strongly at the voxel level and for kurtosis, but does not consistently reduce systematic differences between scanners. As such, it should complement harmonisation, not replace it.

items.title: Jump: Making Large-Scale Connectomics Accessible
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neuroscience, Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Copenhagen, DK-2200 Copenhagen N, Denmark
items.abstract: Large-scale connectomic resources generated from volumetric electron microscopy (EM) have transformed neuroscience by enabling detailed 3D reconstructions of cellular and subcellular morphology and connectivity across hundreds of thousands of cells in diverse tissues and organisms. Recent advances in machine learning-based cell classification and automated segmentation have enabled large-scale annotation of these datasets, yet barriers remain in validating automated classifications and extracting biological insights. To address these challenges, we developed Jump, a suite of user-friendly web-based platforms generated using Claude. These platforms support interactive exploration, expert-guided community review, and quantitative analysis of multiple publicly available EM datasets, while building a growing repository of community-generated annotations. Using uJump, which hosts data from the MICrONS mouse visual cortex dataset, as an example, we demonstrate rapid retrieval of specific cell populations, region-of-interest filtering, biological inspection of cells, and extraction of quantitative morphological and spatial metrics. We showcase analytical features including cell abundance and spatial organisation, connectivity, local cellular neighbourhoods, and volumetric measurements. Using pericytes and endothelial cells as a case study on the cortical vasculature, we further demonstrate how manual review and reclassification can generate accurately identified cell populations for downstream analyses. Consistent with the open-science principles underpinning many large-scale EM resources, Jump is designed to enable broad community participation. By lowering technical barriers to the use of EM datasets, Jump increases analytical efficiency and promotes collaborative efforts to accurately classify cells and structures. Expert-reviewed annotations can be shared across the community, allowing users to build on existing work rather than repeatedly validating the same automated classifications. Collectively, Jump will help researchers to accelerate biological discovery from connectomic datasets.

items.title: Childhood Trauma Severity Compounds Reward Anticipation Disruption in Substance Use Disorders
items.corresponding_institution: Laureate Institute for Brain Research / Oxley College of Health Sciences, University of Tulsa
items.abstract: Background: Substance use disorders (SUD) are associated with reward circuit disruptions and high rates of trauma. Trauma has been found to reduce propensity to engage frontal, limbic, and striatal regions during reward anticipation. However, the interactive effect of trauma and SUD on anticipatory reward circuitry remains unclear. Methods: To address this critical research gap, treatment-enrolled individuals with at least one SUD (N = 150; 78 female) completed questionnaires assessing childhood trauma and current posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and a monetary incentive delay (MID) task during functional magnetic resonance imaging. The MID task presented participants with cues predicting the delivery of no, small, and large monetary gains and avoidance of equally weighted losses. Linear mixed effects models examined the effect of trauma severity or PTSD on percent signal change for anticipation of monetary gains, extracted from a-priori striatal, prefrontal, and mesolimbic anatomic regions of interest. Results: 70.7% of individuals experienced significant childhood trauma and 63.3% met self-report symptom thresholds for probable PTSD. Current PTSD symptoms were positively associated with emotion dysregulation, emotional impulsivity, and drug craving, but were not related to anticipatory BOLD signal. Higher childhood trauma severity (but not current PTSD severity) was associated with lower anticipatory responses within the nucleus accumbens, caudate, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior insula to both gain and loss cues. Conclusions: Childhood adversity is associated with blunted reward anticipation across striatal, prefrontal, and limbic circuitry. This highlights the importance of considering childhood trauma severity in SUD treatment, which may require targeted interventions beyond standard cognitive behavioral therapy to restore normative salience processing, such as striatal neuromodulation.

items.title: Extracellular tumor-derived IL-33 promotes ST2-dependent tumor control
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Tissue Medicine and Pathology, University of Bern, Bern, Switzerland
items.abstract: Interleukin-33 (IL-33) is a pleiotropic cytokine with both nuclear and extracellular functions as well as context-dependent roles in tumor immunity. Although tumor-derived IL-33 can promote anti-tumor immune responses, the contribution of its subcellular localization and extracellular availability to tumor control remains poorly understood. Here, we generated MC38 mouse adenocarcinoma cells overexpressing distinct IL-33 isoforms to dissect the relative contribution of IL-33 nuclear retention versus extracellular activity in a model of heterotopic tumors. Full length IL-33 (FL), an alanine-mutated isoform (Ala) with impaired chromatin binding and a truncated isoform (Trunc) of IL-33 lacking the nuclear functional domains were stably expressed in MC38 cells. These different IL-33 isoforms exhibited distinct subcellular localization and release profiles but had comparable effects on cell proliferation in vitro. In vivo, IL 33 overexpression reduced tumor growth compared with control MC38 cells, with the most pronounced growth impairment observed in tumors expressing Trunc. Trunc tumors also exhibited the highest levels of extracellular IL-33, which was associated with enhanced IFN-{gamma} production and upregulation of the IL-33 receptor ST2 in tumor-infiltrating T cells. Although CD8+ T cells contributed to tumor control, their depletion did not abolish the differential growth between FL- and Ala-expressing tumors, suggesting that additional cell populations contribute to tumor control. However, genetic ablation of St2 abolished the differential tumor growth associated with the IL-33 isoforms, demonstrating that host ST2 signaling is required for isoform-dependent tumor control. Taken together, our findings identify extracellular cytokine availability as a key determinant of the antitumor activity of tumor-derived IL-33 and support a model in which IL-33 promotes ST2-dependent effector T-cell function. Furthermore, our findings highlight intracellular localization versus extracellular release of IL-33 as potential determinants of the context-dependent effects of the IL-33/ST2 axis in cancer.

items.title: Mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) fuels iron-sulfur cluster production essential for type I immunity
items.abstract: Mitochondria orchestrate the metabolic programs that drive T cell-mediated immunity, yet the specific mitochondrial activities that license T cell effector function remain unclear. Here, we identify mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis (mtFAS) as a critical mitochondrial pathway that supports T cell effector function and limits T cell dysfunction. Upon activation, human and mouse T cells robustly induce mtFAS enzymes in a Myc-dependent manner. Disrupting mtFAS activity in T cells through deletion of the initiating enzyme, malonyl-CoA-acyl carrier protein transacylase (MCAT), sharply reduces effector cytokine production and impairs type I immunity, including CD8+ cytotoxic and CD4+ Th1 responses, to bacterial and viral pathogens in vivo. Loss of MCAT disrupts protein lipoylation and iron-sulfur cluster (ISC) production in T cells, disrupting the stability and function of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Deletion of ISC biosynthesis machinery phenocopies MCAT loss, whereas selective disruption of protein lipoylation does not. Moreover, selective restoration of protein lipoylation in MCAT-deficient T cells fails to rescue effector function, establishing ISC biogenesis and its downstream support of ETC activity as the principal mtFAS-dependent mechanism sustaining T cell effector function. MCAT deficiency also promotes the premature acquisition of exhaustion-associated features in CD8+ T cells, including increased PD-1 and TIM-3 expression and reduced cytokine competence. Together, these findings establish mtFAS as an essential pathway for initiating and sustaining T cell effector responses, identifying ISC biogenesis and ETC activity as core mtFAS-dependent outputs critical for T cell effector responses and resistance to exhaustion.

items.title: Structural basis of human antibody recognition of linear and conformational epitopes on the peanut allergen Ara h 2
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: IgE-mediated food allergy requires allergens to crosslink FcERI-bound IgE on mast cells, yet how individual allergen epitopes organize pathogenic IgE complexes remains poorly understood. We defined the structural basis of antibody recognition of Ara h 2, a major peanut allergen, using three human monoclonal antibodies isolated from IgG1 memory B cells of peanut-allergic children. As IgE, the DPYSPS repeat-specific antibody P4EC10 alone induced degranulation in vitro and passive cutaneous anaphylaxis in vivo, whereas P1BC6 and P1EC5 elicited both responses only when combined. P4EC10 IgG1 inhibited a mean of 46% of Ara h 2 binding to plasma IgE in the highest Ara h 2-specific IgE stratum and 24% in the lowest. Cryo-EM revealed 2:1 and 3:1 P4EC10 Fab-Ara h 2 complexes. In the 2:1 structure, two Fabs bound adjacent linear DPYSPS repeats within the flexible loop and contacted one another. P1BC6 and P1EC5 each bound Ara h 2 with 1:1 stoichiometry and simultaneously engaged distinct conformational epitopes. Solution binding measurements supported these stoichiometries and indicated that proline hydroxylation enhanced P4EC10 binding. These findings show that Ara h 2 can drive effector-cell activation by recruiting a single IgE specificity to repeated epitopes or by engaging distinct IgE specificities at separate conformational epitopes.

items.title: Recognition of β-D-glucose by surfactant protein D and structural evidence for an extended carbohydrate binding site
items.abstract: Human surfactant protein D (hSP-D) is an innate immune protein involved in pathogen recognition in the lungs. Structural definition of the recognition of small carbohydrates by rfhSP-D, a biologically and therapeutically active recombinant homotrimeric fragment of hSP-D, has previously revealed the details of calcium dependent binding in the carbohydrate recognition domain and the influence of residues flanking the binding pocket. To provide further structural insight into pathogen exo-polysaccharide recognition by hSP-D and the impact of alternative anomers and linkages, we have used x-ray crystallography and a competitive mannan-based ELISA to investigate the binding of -D-glucose chains (3-7 sugars) and of {beta}-linked glucose trisaccharides derived from long-chain cell wall components of fungal species and allergenic plant components and from extracellular matrices of bacterial biofilms. Our results reveal that a variety of determinants influence the binding configuration, and that SP-D can recognise reducing terminal {beta}-D-glucose through calcium mediated coordination of the O2' and O1' hydroxyls, with the flexibility to recognise alternative epitopes when the preferred target is unavailable for binding. The ligands based on naturally occurring exo-polysaccharides reveal variable, novel and flexible recognition by hSP-D. {beta}-cellotriose and {beta}-laminaritriose exhibit different {beta}-glucose binding modes (non-reducing O3', O4 ' and reducing O1', O2 ' respectively), both with moderate affinity for rfhSP-D. The high affinity {beta}-isomaltotriose ligand binds via the reducing terminal {beta}-glucose O2' and O1' in the calcium-binding pocket, supplemented by interaction of the internal, non-terminal glucose with an extended binding surface, revealing a potential mechanism for high affinity dual-site recognition of extended dextrans.

items.title: Transient fetal type 2 bovine viral diarrhea virus infection protects beef cattle from postnatal challenge with type 1b bovine viral diarrhea virus and Mannheimia haemolytica
items.abstract: Bovine respiratory disease (BRD) is the most significant disease in feedlot cattle, impacting animal growth, performance, and profitability. Acute bovine viral diarrhea virus (BVDV) infections have been shown to increase the occurrence of BRD. Fetal infection with BVDV during late gestation results in transient fetal infections (TI). At birth, TI calves are negative for BVDV but positive for BVDV-specific antibodies. The objective of this experiment was to determine the effect of TI status on the susceptibility to BRD and the subsequent rate of gain in feedlot cattle. Eight-month-old type 2 BVDV TI and uninfected control heifers (TI-BRD n=5; CON-BRD n=6) were challenged with an intranasal inoculation of non-cytopathogenic (ncp) type 1b BVDV, followed by an intratracheal inoculation with Mannheimia haemolytica. TI and uninfected heifers (TI-CON n=6; CON-CON n=5) were sham-inoculated with media and phosphate buffered saline (PBS) to serve as BRD challenge controls. Heifers were weighed at the beginning and end of the experiment, were evaluated daily for clinical signs of respiratory disease, and jugular blood samples were collected on d 0, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 17, and 31 post-BVDV inoculation. Complete blood count (CBC), flow cytometry, BVDV RTPCR, and serum neutralizing antibody titers for type 1b and type 2 BVDV were measured in blood and serum samples. Average daily gain was similar across treatments. Fetal infection with ncp type 2 BVDV in late gestation resulted in cross-protective immunity, which reduced (P < 0.05) clinical scores, lymphopenia, and viremia in TI heifers following postnatal challenge with a noncytopathic type 1b BVDV and Mannheimia haemolytica compared to challenged control heifers. These findings indicate that fetal BVDV TI may protect offspring from the deleterious effects of combined type 1b BVDV and Mannheimia haemolytica infection during the postnatal period.

items.title: MALT1 is an E3 ligase catalyzing its own activation by monoubiquitination
items.abstract: The protease mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma translocation protein-1 (MALT1) is an important signaling component of the antigen receptor-induced activation of lymphocytes. Abnormal MALT1 activity is linked to emergence of several lymphoma subtypes. Humans and mice with inactivating MALT1 mutations, on the other hand, show defects in specific classes of immune cells and develop autoimmunity. MALT1 protease activity depends on its inducible K644-monoubiquitination. We have previously identified a negatively charged ubiquitin binding site in MALT1, located ~30[A] from K644, that is necessary for MALT1 monoubiquitination. However, the machinery delivering activated ubiquitin to MALT1 and transferring it to K644 remains unknown. Here we provide evidence that MALT1 is an E3-ligase catalyzing autoubiquitination via a cascade involving MALT1 residue C687, accepting ubiquitin from a ubiquitinated E2-enzyme, and transferring that active ubiquitin to the MALT1 monoubiquitination site, K644. We further identified MALT1 residue Y631, which lies between MALT1(C687) and MALT1(K644), as a gatekeeper of this process. Lymphocyte lines expressing MALT1(C687A) or MALT1(Y631A) mutants showed impaired or increased activation, respectively. Finally, we identified Ube2L3 as a candidate cysteine-specific E2-enzyme servicing MALT1. Overexpression of inactive Ube2L3 compromised MALT1 monoubiquitination and protease activity, indicating Ube2L3 inhibition is a potential means to dampen MALT1 ubiquitination. Collectively, the findings identify MALT1 as an E3 ligase capable of catalyzing its own activation through auto-ubiquitination, which may open new avenues for therapeutic regulation of MALT1 activity.

items.title: Host glycans trap bacterial lectins to trigger NLRP3 inflammasome activation
items.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa poses a severe threat to immunocompromised patients through its multifaceted virulence arsenal. Although diverse bacterial components activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, the precise molecular triggers driving this process remain largely elusive. Here, we reveal that host surface glycans effectively trap the P. aeruginosa lectins LecA and LecB, initiating carbohydrate-dependent inflammasome activation. This lectin-mediated cascade exhibits striking host-species and cell-type specificity. The L-fucose-specific LecB activates human blood monocytes and THP-1 cells, where glycosylated {beta}1-integrin contributes to signal transduction, whereas the D-galactose-specific LecA is more potent in murine bone marrow-derived macrophages and dendritic cells. This mechanism requires potassium efflux and displays cell-specific sensitivity to reactive oxygen species. Infection with live bacteria recapitulates the lectin-mediated inflammasome response. Collectively, our findings unveil an unexpected role for host glycans as critical, previously overlooked checkpoints gating P. aeruginosa-driven inflammation, offering fresh insights into host-pathogen dynamics and exposing novel therapeutic targets.

items.title: Longitudinal multiomics analysis in blood from individuals before and after HIV acquisition
items.abstract: A comprehensive understanding of cellular immunity is essential for controlling viral infections, yet individual and coordinated immune responses continue to pose significant challenges in HIV cure research. Recent advances in single-cell and multiomics technologies provide powerful tools to dissect intricate multicellular behaviors and identify novel therapeutic targets. Direct characterization of HIV-induced immune alterations is challenging because matched samples obtained before HIV acquisition are rare. To better understand individual and coordinated cellular immune responses relevant to HIV cure research, we integrated single-nucleus chromatin-accessibility and transcriptomic profiling of 150,060 PBMCs with plasma metabolome, lipidome and soluble immune-profiling from five individuals before HIV acquisition, during early infection and after at least six months of suppressive antiretroviral therapy (ART). HIV acquisition expanded activated CD8 T and proliferating NK/CD8 T cells and induced cell-type-specific chromatin and transcriptional changes enriched for interferon, inflammatory and TNF-NF-{kappa}B programs, many persisting during ART. Multiome sequencing detected 32 HIV-positive cells which were associated with increased expression of IFI44L during early infection and ATAD3A after ART. Plasma IP-10 increased transiently, whereas eight energy- or amino-acid-related metabolites showed nominal decreases persisting after ART. These paired observations distinguish transient inflammatory responses from persistent molecular and metabolic perturbations after HIV acquisition.

items.title: Tnfrsf13b Variants Enhance IgG-Mediated Complement Responses to Promote Bacterial Clearance
items.abstract: RSF13B encodes the TACI receptor, necessary for differentiation of B cells into plasma cells. TNFRSF13B is highly polymorphic, yet common non-synonymous variants including those that impair the receptor structure and/or signaling are retained in the population. Here we show that mice carrying the Tnfrsf13b A144E variant, the murine homolog of the human TNFRSF13B A181E variant associated with common variable immunodeficiency, effectively clear host-adapted Citrobacter rodentium (a murine model of pathogenic E. coli infection) despite nine-fold decreased bacteria-specific IgG compared to WT mice. IgG from Tnfrsf13b mutant mice exhibited reduced sialic acid, terminal galactose, fucose, and showed enhanced complement effector functions, including greater C1q binding and membrane attack complex (C5b) deposition. Results show that some Tnfrsf13b variants enhance complement-dependent antibody effector function, thereby identifying TACI as a regulator of IgG effector properties and providing a potential explanation for the evolutionary persistence of TNFRSF13B mutations.

items.title: Lipin-1-cardiolipin axis sustains mitochondrial respiration and efferocytosis in macrophages
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Louisiana State University Health Sciences Center, Shreveport, LA 71103, United States
items.abstract: Defective macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells contributes to persistent inflammation and cardiometabolic disease. Efferocytosis requires mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, but how macrophages maintain respiratory capacity during resolution remains unclear. Here, we show that lipin-1 supports efferocytosis through a cardiolipin-associated mitochondrial program. In IL-4-stimulated macrophages, lipin-1 deficiency reduced cardiolipin abundance and selectively lowered the abundance of inner mitochondrial membrane proteins, including respiratory-chain components, consistent with decreased mitochondrial respiratory capacity. These defects occurred without broad suppression of canonical metabolic transcriptional programs, and experimentally altering mitochondrial morphology failed to reproduce or rescue the functional phenotype. Disrupting cardiolipin synthesis impaired efferocytosis, whereas the cardiolipin-interacting peptide SS-31 improved mitochondrial respiration and apoptotic-cell clearance in lipin-1-deficient macrophages. Systemic SS-31 treatment also reduced apoptotic-cell accumulation after dexamethasone-induced thymic injury. Together, these findings implicate cardiolipin homeostasis in lipin-1-dependent macrophage bioenergetics and efferocytosis, identifying a potentially actionable pathway while leaving the mechanism connecting lipin-1 to cardiolipin abundance unresolved.

items.title: Single-cell T cell receptor sequencing deciphers αβ- and γδ-T cell responses in neuroblastoma
authors: van der Steeg, A. F. W.
items.corresponding_institution: Princess Maxima Center for Pediatric Oncology, Utrecht, the Netherlands
items.abstract: High-risk neuroblastoma is a pediatric tumor with poor survival rates and low MHC-I expression. The cellular determinants of anti-tumor immunity remain poorly defined, limiting development of targeted immunotherapies. We generated a single-cell atlas integrating transcriptomic and {beta}/{gamma}{delta} T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing of >150,000 T cells from tumor and blood of 10 patients throughout treatment. Fractions of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells are clonally expanded and activated, with tumor-specific expansion among CD4+ cells. Transcriptomic evidence of tumor-reactivity is more pronounced in CD4+ than CD8+ T cells. Moreover, V{delta}1+ {gamma}{delta}T cells are enriched, displaying TCR engagement. Functional screening confirmed reactivity of selected {gamma}{delta}TCRs and, remarkably, a small fraction of CD8+ {beta}TCRs. Subset-specific inhibitory receptors, including CTLA4, FCRL6, and KIRs, may serve as targets for tailored immunotherapies. Together, we identify distinct {beta}- and {gamma}{delta}T cell responses despite low MHC-I, and provide a comprehensive resource for deciphering pediatric immunity against MHC-Ilow tumors.

items.title: SimpleP2G: Importance of Image Encoders for Gene Expression Prediction from Pathology Images
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China
items.abstract: Pathology-image-to-gene-expression (P2G) studies often change the prediction head, image encoder, and spatial context together, making performance differences difficult to attribute. We examine these factors through paired image-input controls and explicit input regimes. Our main comparison covers five HEST-1K datasets, two 200-gene panels, and three selected held-out slides per dataset, using validation-selected checkpoints. Across all five datasets, replacing conventional image inputs with Virchow2 improves mean PCC-200 in 39 of 40 method--dataset--panel comparisons, while one comparison decreases. We introduce SimpleP2G, a direct gene-query decoder over frozen embeddings, and SimpleP2G-cross, which adds spatially positioned neighboring embeddings. With shared Virchow2 features, SimpleP2G has the highest single-patch mean PCC-200 on all five datasets under both panels; the cross-patch variant leads on four of five datasets under each panel. Decoder and context ablations show that greater depth and broader context do not consistently improve prediction. Together, these results suggest improving image representations before adding prediction-head complexity: a direct decoder over frozen pathology embeddings already provides a strong baseline. We hope our reimplemented image-encoder-upgraded baselines and SimpleP2G models serve as transparent, reproducible, and strong controls for future P2G research.

items.title: Spatial dissection of a megabase-scale gene in Drosophila spermatocyte nuclei
items.abstract: Understanding how nascent RNA is structurally organized during transcription remains challenging for most genes because their transcription units are too small to resolve the spatial organization of nascent transcripts. Exceptionally long genes provide a unique opportunity to address how RNA is organized during transcription. Here, we investigate the transcriptional organization of kl-3, an exceptionally long Y-linked fertility gene expressed in Drosophila spermatocytes. Using RNA FISH against AATAC satellite sequence embedded in a large intron (intron5), we find that nascent exon-containing transcripts remain tightly associated with the Y-loop DNA strand, whereas intronic transcripts form a distinct outer layer surrounding the exon-associated signal. We further demonstrate that Smooth protein associates specifically with the AATAC positive loop, and is required for proper transcript organization, likely by creating phase-separated compartments. Finally, we identify distinct subnuclear localization of transcription-, elongation-, and splicing-machineries. H3K4me3 is enriched near the nucleolus-like body (NLB), consistent with transcriptional initiation in this region.
