Guided by RSC, we designed a pairwise difference loss between neighboring spots that improved fine-scale predictions on average across 11 models. RSC thus provides a foundation for benchmarking predictions, guiding model design and determining which spatial analyses histology can support.

items.title: Genome-guided vs transcriptome-guided mapping: systematic evaluation of RNA-seq quantification bias for tandemly duplicated genes in model and crop plants
items.corresponding_institution: Kunpeng Institute of Modern Agriculture at Foshan
items.abstract: Accurate quantification of RNA-seq data is fundamental to modern plant biology. The choice of mapping strategy and aligner critically determines expression quantification accuracy and shapes the quality of downstream biological analyses. However, a pervasive yet often underappreciated challenge is the accurate quantification of genes located within tandemly duplicated arrays. Here, we selected six representative plant species (Arabidopsis thaliana and five important crops), and compared RNA-seq analysis results generated from two mapping strategies (genome-guided and transcriptome-guided) using three widely used aligners (TopHat2, HISAT2, and STAR). Our results reveal pervasive alignment errors in genome-guided strategies, arising primarily from misaligned reads spanning tandem gene duplicates, a gene class that plays important roles in plant defense and stress responses, detoxification, and secondary metabolism. TopHat2 with the transcriptome-guided strategy yielded the most accurate alignments, whereas transcriptome-guided HISAT2 and STAR corrected most, but not all, of the errors. Transcriptome-guided mapping also demonstrates superior performance over the genome-guided approach on simulated RNA-seq benchmark datasets. Moreover, in functional enrichment analysis, the transcriptome-guided strategy outperformed the genome-guided one in retrieving gene sets biologically relevant to the processes under study. Overall, this study provides a systematic evaluation of how mapping strategies and software selections affect RNA-seq quantification for tandem gene duplicates, and offers a valuable reference for standardizing plant RNA-seq analytical workflows, particularly for studies investigating biology processes regulated by tandem gene duplicates.

items.title: BRIDGE: Backbone Representation for Inverse-folding-Driven Generalizable RNA Encoding
items.abstract: RNA recognizes small molecules and proteins through their three dimensional structures, but sparse functional annotations limit task specific learning of transferable structural features. We present BRIDGE, an inverse-folding encoder pretrained on 2,501 RNA chain records from experimental structures. Each nucleotide is represented by its phosphorus atom and five ribose atoms (P, C1', C2', C3', C4', O4'). Base coordinates are not encoder inputs. From these atoms, the encoder is trained to predict nucleotide identity, solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and base geometry. With matched readouts, frozen BRIDGE representations reach a three-model ensemble pooled average precision (AP) of 0.627 for external ligand-binding site prediction and 0.647 for RNA-protein interface prediction, compared with 0.503 and 0.516 for frozen, randomly initialized encoders. Under the evaluated full-adaptation recipes, pretrained initialization reaches AP 0.703 for ligand binding and 0.641 for protein interfaces, versus 0.635 and 0.623 for training from scratch. Sequence-only pretraining, without SASA or base-geometry targets, also transfers to both tasks. Whether the base-geometry objectives add further value depends on the task and adaptation mode. In decoy ranking and apo/holo evaluations, transfer depends on the readout and the test set, and small target panels and downstream training overlap in the apo/holo evaluation limit broader conclusions. These results support inverse-folding pretraining as a route to transferable RNA structural representations that do not require observed base coordinates at inference.

items.title: Beyond IgG: Oral Secretory IgA as a new efficient modality for cancer immunotherapy
items.abstract: Monoclonal antibody therapies have revolutionized cancer treatment but are almost exclusively based on intravenously administered IgG antibodies. Here, we developed and evaluated the first orally delivered anti-CEACAM5 secretory IgA (SIgA) for colorectal cancer. The pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, antitumor efficacy and immune effects of oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) were evaluated in an orthotopic metastatic human colorectal cancer model. Its therapeutic activity was compared with cetuximab, as monotherapy and in combination with irinotecan- or FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy along with that of an anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 sharing the same antigen-binding domain. Tumor-associated FcRI (CD89)-expressing myeloid populations were characterized at primary and metastatic sites. ABC-101 activity was evaluated on a second human cancer cell line, in vivo in an orthotopic human gastric cancer model. Oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) exhibited a unique pharmacokinetic profile, selectively accumulating in CEACAM5-positive primary tumors and metastases while maintaining minimal systemic exposure. Compared with the anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 and cetuximab, oral SIgA achieved superior inhibition of primary tumor growth and metastatic dissemination. It also enhanced the efficacy of irinotecan- and FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy, outperforming the FOLFIRI/cetuximab standard-of-care comparator. Mechanistically, ABC-101 remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting the recruitment of FcRI (CD89)-expressing neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells at both primary and metastatic sites, consistent with enhanced innate antitumor activity. Oral ABC-101 shows targeted activity against CEAhigh MKN-45 cells, reducing markers of cell proliferation and migration. These findings establish therapeutic SIgA as a first-in-class oral antibody immunotherapy combining selective tumor targeting, innate immune activation, and enhanced chemotherapy efficacy. More broadly, this work establishes mucosal immunity as a promising therapeutic frontier, demonstrating that orally delivered antibodies can enable systemic control of metastatic digestive cancers.

items.title: Ecological Feedback Dimensionality and Trade-Off Shape Govern Cancer Phenotypic Diversification
items.corresponding_institution: City St George's, University of London
items.abstract: Cancer cells face a variety of trade-offs in their microenvironment, from competition vs. colonization to immune evasion vs. rapid proliferation. Whether such trade-offs drive cancer cell populations to a single optimal phenotype or to a stable coexistence of phenotypes depends on the trade-off's shape and the number of independent ecological feedbacks that cells impose on each other and on their environment. We introduce trade-off and invasion plots (TIPs), a geometric tool from adaptive dynamics that determines the evolutionary outcome from the curvature of a trade-off relative to a pair of invasion boundaries, to cancer and ground our analysis in simple consumer-resource metabolic models. We show that the dimension of the ecological feedback determines whether diversification can occur: a one-dimensional feedback leads to monomorphism, whereas a two-dimensional feedback can promote evolutionary branching to a stable dimorphism. Furthermore, we show that the curvature of the allocation trade-off governs whether a single metabolic generalist (attractor), a stable dimorphism of specialists (evolutionary branching), or a single specialist (repellor) occurs. Both results are cancer-specific instances of long-established principles in theoretical ecology, namely the bound that the dimension of the feedback environment places on coexistence, and the fitness-set geometry relating trade-off curvature to specialization. Our contribution therefore primarily lies in bringing this mature eco-evolutionary machinery to bear on intratumoral heterogeneity.

items.title: Multimodal Virtual Screening Identifies Candidate Inhibitors of Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells Across Breast Cancer Subtypes
items.corresponding_institution: UPMC Hillman Cancer Center/University of Pittsburgh
items.abstract: Polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) are associated with treatment resistance and tumor recurrence yet identifying compounds that selectively suppress these cells remains challenging. Here, we developed a multimodal machine-learning framework to prioritize PGCC-suppressing compounds by integrating chemical fingerprints, drug-induced cellular morphology, transcriptomic perturbation profiles, and biologically informed molecular annotations. Using screening data from four breast cancer cell lines, we systematically evaluated feature selection, drug representations, and ensemble learning strategies. PGCC-guided feature selection reduced morphology dimensionality by 93.7% while identifying cell-cycle-enriched gene sets, linking predictive features to biologically relevant processes. An ensemble integrating complementary predictors achieved a mean Pearson correlation of 0.403 and an enrichment factor of 5.46 among the top 5% of ranked compounds. In held-out screening data, the ensemble recovered 27.9% of experimentally identified hits, representing approximately 5.6-fold and 2.5-fold improvements over random selection and the best individual predictor, respectively. We subsequently prioritized 21,367 compounds from an external library for experimental evaluation. Experimental testing identified six candidates that preferentially suppressed PGCCs in at least three paclitaxel-treated cell lines. Notably, AZD-8055 and voxtalisib reduced PGCC abundance by at least 70% across all four cell lines. These results establish a multimodal computational-experimental strategy for phenotype-directed drug discovery and provide new candidates for targeting treatment-induced PGCCs.

items.title: FN1 is produced by cancer-associated fibroblasts and carries no immune-exclusion signal beyond the collagen program: a two-cohort single-cell re-examination in non-small cell lung cancer
items.abstract: Fibronectin 1 (FN1) has been proposed as a macrophage-derived driver of T-cell exclusion and AP-1-mediated resistance to checkpoint blockade in lung cancer. The human evidence was never tested against the two confounders most likely to generate them: collagen/extracellular-matrix (ECM) abundance and dissociation-induced immediate-early gene (IEG) expression. We reanalyzed two public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cohorts, GSE148071 (42 treatment-naive tumors) and GSE207422 (15 specimens; 92,330 cells), with 24 pre-treatment bulk transcriptomes. Malignant epithelium was called by compartment-level inferCNV; FN1 source was attributed within macrophage and fibroblast compartments and by ligand-receptor scoring; exclusion associations were tested by partial Spearman correlation with permutation testing, controlling for a 22-gene collagen/ECM signature; AP-1 regulon activity was quantified before and after masking the 27-gene IEG panel, benchmarked against a dissociation-stress score. FN1 was produced predominantly by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs): the FN1-positive fraction was higher in CAFs than macrophages in both cohorts (paired Wilcoxon P = 1.6 x 10?? and P = 0.002), and CAF-to-epithelium communication exceeded macrophage-to-epithelium by about six-fold (median 0.32 vs 0.05, P = 1.5 x 10??). An independent lung-adenocarcinoma cohort (GSE131907) replicated this cell of origin (FN1-positive fraction 0.88 in CAFs versus 0.44 in TAMs; 11 paired samples, P = 0.001). The bulk FN1-cytotoxic association ({rho} = -0.53, P = 0.008) disappeared after collagen adjustment across three independent FN1 scoring schemes (partial {rho} = +0.21 to -0.16, all P > 0.33) and was not reproduced at single-cell level. Sample-level AP-1 activity tracked dissociation stress ({rho} = 0.88, P = 2.3 x 10??); IEG masking shrank histology-associated effect sizes by 40-64%, yet masked activity remained stress-coupled ({rho} = 0.82). FN1 is therefore a CAF product whose apparent link to immune exclusion is absorbed by the collagen program, and AP-1 readouts from dissociated tissue are stress-dominated; stress scores should accompany AP-1-based resistance claims.

items.title: Single-agent PD-L1 blockade and tumour volume in orthotopic GL261 glioma, with an exploratory lipid analysis of the treated tumours
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has not yet changed outcomes in glioblastoma (GBM), and in immunocompetent mouse glioma the effect of a single blocking antibody is usually reported as survival rather than as tumour volume with its own confidence interval. We treated mice bearing orthotopic GL261 gliomas with anti-PD-L1 as a single agent in an IDH1-wild-type and in an IDH1-mutant line, and followed tumour volume by MRI. At day 14, tumours of treated animals were 0.33 times the volume of control tumours in the IDH1-wild-type line (95 % CI 0.21 to 0.53; p < 0.001; 16 anti-PD-L1 and 20 control animals) and 0.42 times in the IDH1-mutant line (0.22 to 0.78; p = 0.006; 10 and 10 animals), from a linear mixed model of log tumour volume over days 8 to 16. Diffusion imaging of the same tumours gave a higher apparent diffusion coefficient in the treated IDH1-wild-type tumours, by 23 % over the whole tumour (p = 0.027), and lower fractional anisotropy in the treated IDH1-mutant tumours, by 25 % over the whole tumour (p = 0.023), and in the periphery of the IDH1-wild-type ones, by 24 % (p = 0.005). We also imaged the lipid composition of treated and control IDH1-wild-type tumours ex vivo by mass spectrometry imaging: relative to the healthy brain of the same section, sphingomyelin was higher in the treated tumours and phosphatidylcholine species shifted towards shorter chains (p = 0.016 for both). In orthotopic GL261 glioma, anti-PD-L1 as a single agent reduces tumour volume in the IDH1-wild-type and in the IDH1-mutant line.

items.title: The PD-L1 metabolic interactome in glioma is bounded by IDH1 genotype
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has failed in glioblastoma, and part of the reason may lie in the tumour cell itself: if the checkpoint and the metabolism that sustains the cell hold each other up, then lowering one arm hands the tumour the other, and a single agent cannot win. We tested that possibility in GL261 glioma cells of IDH1-wildtype and IDH1-mutant genotype, silencing Chka or Cd274, blocking PD-L1 with an antibody, and reading the consequences by RT-qPCR, RNA sequencing, flow cytometry of surface PD-L1 and high-resolution 1H NMR of dual-phase cell extracts. The two genes proved reciprocal in both genotypes: silencing either transcript raised the other, and silencing choline kinase roughly doubled PD-L1 at the cell surface. Antibody blockade did something the silencing did not. In IDH1-wildtype cells it lowered soluble phosphocholine, the only one of twenty-two aqueous signals to survive correction for multiple testing, and raised total lipid per cell without changing lipid composition, whereas silencing PD-L1 raised phosphocholine instead; in IDH1-mutant cells neither change occurred. The transcriptome drew the same boundary, engaging a sterol programme and lowering glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation in wild-type cells only. The interferon response did not respect that boundary and rose under every perturbation in both genotypes. Removing PD-L1 from inside the cell and blocking it from outside are therefore not the same intervention, and the metabolic half of the response stops at the IDH1 genotype.

items.title: Development of a Novel Multitarget Directed Ligand (MTDL), LCI132 for the Polypharmaceutical Treatment of High-Risk MYCN Amplified Neuroblastoma
items.corresponding_institution: Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Comprehensive Cancer Center/Levine Cancer Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina, 28204, USA
items.abstract: MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma (MNA-NB) is associated with poor prognosis due to the development of resistance to current aggressive therapy and to the subsequent limited response to single agent targeted therapeutics in the relapse setting. Herein, we describe the in silico design and development of the first-in-class nanomolar potent, selective, multitarget directed ligand (MTDL) against PI3K, BRD4, CDK4/6/9 and Aurora kinases A/B, LCI132, for the polypharmaceutical treatment of MNA-NB. LCI132 demonstrates a favorable safety and pharmacokinetics profile, suppresses viability, induces apoptosis in MNA-NB and inhibits in vivo tumor growth with no toxicity. Mechanistically our data show that LCI132 orthogonally inhibits MYCN transcription and induces proteasome mediated MYCN degradation. We and others recently observed an augmented cytostatic effect of combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with retinoic acid in MNA-NB models and the associated disruption of core regulatory circuits. Importantly, this was not associated with the induction of apoptosis. The combined treatment of MNA-NB cells with retinoic acid and LCI132 synergistically inhibited cellular proliferation and induced apoptosis in MNA-NB cell lines and ex vivo patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Combination of LCI132 and ATRA treatment effectively reduces levels of MYCN and alters the expression of CRC transcription factors. Collectively, our study provides mechanistic insights and a rationale for the combined use of ATRA and a MTDL, LCI132 as a novel polypharmaceutical therapeutic strategy for the treatment of MNA-NB NB.

items.title: Discovery of latent clinical phenotypes through optimal transport of brain dynamics
items.corresponding_institution: Department of General Psychology, University of Padova, Padova, Italy
items.abstract: The increasing availability of large clinical neuroimaging datasets has enabled the discovery of objective, data-driven clinical phenotypes. However, current approaches typically rely on structural or static functional metrics, thereby overlooking the rich information embedded in brain dynamics. To address this limitation, we developed a computational framework combining a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) with Optimal Transport (OT) theory. By representing individual brain dynamics within a shared latent state space, our approach quantifies how much one subject's state-transition dynamics would need to be modified to match another subject's state occupancy distribution, providing a pairwise measure of inter-individual variability that captures temporal aspects of brain function. We applied this framework to multiple sclerosis (MS), a condition where substantial within-group heterogeneity challenges traditional clinical classification. Analyzing resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 122 patients with relapsing-remitting MS and 97 matched healthy controls, the HMM identified three latent states with distinct connectivity patterns. While patients showed an altered temporal organization of recurrent brain states relative to healthy controls, reflected in selective differences in state occupancy and dwell time, we focused on quantifying heterogeneity specifically within the MS cohort. Clustering patients according to OT-based dissimilarities revealed two subgroups with distinct clinical disability and structural disease burden. Crucially, this stratification was not detectable when applying clustering procedures to static functional connectivity, supporting the added value of dynamical features. Our results establish a general methodological framework for extracting clinically relevant phenotypes from temporal brain dynamics, with potential applications across neurological and psychiatric conditions characterized by phenotypic heterogeneity.

items.title: Latent state selection, not outcome integration, resolves approach-avoidance conflict
items.corresponding_institution: Amsterdam UMC location VUmc, Anatomy & Neurosciences, De Boelelaan 1108, 1081 HZ Amsterdam, The Netherlands
items.abstract: Appropriate action selection under approach-avoidance is crucial for survival and emotional resilience. Tasks designed to measure this conflict typically observe response rates at an intermediate rate. However, whether this reflects a single compromised policy or alternation between opposing strategies is unresolved. We trained rats on a novel three trial operant conflict task and recorded anterior insular cortex (aIC) activity with fiber photometry. Fitting a cross-validated GLM-HMM to trial-by-trial choices identified three discrete latent states: a risk-taking state in which rats responded on most conflict trials, a risk-averse state in which they withheld on most conflict trials, and a perseverative state. Rather than integrating the two possible outcomes in conflict, aIC activity flexibly adjusted according to the active state, such that it resembled reward trials in the risk-taking state and punishment trials in the risk-averse state. We also found that acute alcohol increased punished responses by shifting state occupancy. In a yoked Pavlovian cohort, anticipatory aIC signals were reduced, indicating that this encoding requires instrumental agency. Together, these findings suggest that approach-avoidance conflict is resolved by selection between discrete strategies, and that insular recruitment of this process depends on the capacity to act.

items.title: Influence of Memory Modulation on Affective States in Methamphetamine Use Disorder
items.corresponding_institution: Laureate Institute for Brain Research / Oxley College of Health Sciences, University of Tulsa
items.abstract: Background: Negative affect and low positive affect are linked to craving and relapse in methamphetamine use disorder (MUD). Brief positive autobiographical memory recall improves mood in non-clinical samples, but it has not been tested in people in treatment for MUD. We tested whether positive memory recall improves affective state, withdrawal and craving compared with a neutral recall condition. Methods: Adults with past-year MUD in their first year of abstinence were recruited from two residential treatment programs in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Participants were randomized, blinded to condition, to recall personally meaningful positive memories (Positive; n = 37) or emotionally neutral procedural memories (Procedural; n = 36) during a laboratory session. Positive and negative affect (PANAS, the prespecified primary outcomes), withdrawal (AWQ), craving (visual digital scale; Stimulant Craving Questionnaire), and anhedonia (SHAPS) were assessed before and approximately one hour after the recall. Group x Time effects were tested with mixed ANCOVAs adjusted for sex and age, with Holm and false discovery rate correction. Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were estimated for each outcome. Results: Of 80 randomized participants, 73 began the session and were analyzed. The Group x Time interaction was not significant for positive affect (p = .689) or negative affect (p = .399). Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were small and imprecise (positive affect: -0.53 points, 95% CI -2.60 to 1.53; negative affect: 0.54 points, 95% CI -0.90 to 1.99). Across both groups, negative affect, withdrawal, craving and desire to use decreased over the session, while positive affect also declined (all p [≤] .015). No secondary or exploratory outcome differed between conditions. Conclusions: A single positive autobiographical memory recall did not produce a detectable end-of-session difference in affect, withdrawal or craving relative to neutral recall in individuals with MUD. Affective and craving states shifted across the session regardless of memory content. Future work should test repeated or more intensive positive-affect interventions in this population.

items.title: Sleep EEG distinguishes learned from novel auditory cues without predicting memory retention in a targeted memory reactivation study
items.abstract: Memory consolidation during sleep is thought to build on processes initiated during encoding, but how encoding-related brain activity affects individual memories during sleep is unknown. Using targeted memory reactivation (TMR), we tested whether auditory cues elicit memory-related responses during sleep, whether encoding theta and delta power predict these responses, and whether encoding- and sleep-related measures predict long-term retention. Eighty-one healthy young adults learned sound-associated item-face/place pairs during electroencephalography (EEG). Memory was tested before sleep, 12 hours, and 5 days after encoding. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, a subset of learned sounds and novel control sounds were replayed. Item-level mixed-effects models assessed behavioural and EEG predictors of retention success, and item-level correlations related encoding to cue-induced power during sleep. Pre-sleep memory strength and encoding vividness predicted retention, with the vividness effect depending on encoding theta power. TMR did not improve memory and was associated with poorer retention of initially weak memories. Learned cues elicited stronger delta responses than novel sounds during sleep, yet cue-induced delta, theta, and sigma power did not predict retention. Encoding and sleep EEG power were unrelated and showed distinct scalp topographies. In a large item-level dataset, the sleeping brain distinguished learned from novel cues, but this processing did not translate into durable retention, which was instead determined at encoding. Encoding-related oscillations did not relate to memories preferentially reactivated or strengthened by sleep cueing. These findings caution against treating cue-induced sleep oscillations as markers of successful reactivation or consolidation.

items.title: Connectomic Flow Across Cortical Sensory Systems in Juvenile Fibromyalgia
items.abstract: Adult fibromyalgia (FM) is characterized by altered functional connectivity between sensory, salience, and default mode networks (DMN), yet its early emergence and hierarchical organization remain unclear in Juvenile Fibromyalgia (JFM). We used stepwise functional connectivity (SFC) to detect early changes in the hierarchical integration of sensory signals toward salience and heteromodal networks in adolescents with JFM. Additionally, we assessed whether these alterations overlap with FM-associated gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA). Forty-six adolescent females with JFM (16.44-1.11 years) and forty-three healthy females (16.09-1.06 years) completed clinical questionnaires and underwent resting-state fMRI. Whole-brain voxel-wise SFC mapped connectivity patterns from primary sensory regions (visual, somatosensory, auditory) toward the DMN across increasing link-step distances. Regression models examined associations between symptom severity and SFC measures. Spatial overlap between functional findings and FM-associated gene expression profiles was also evaluated. Both groups showed a similar pattern, progressing from primary to secondary sensory regions, then to multimodal integration and salience areas, and finally to heteromodal DMN cortices. Greater symptom severity was associated with reduced second-step connectivity between secondary somatosensory cortices and the right anterior insula/operculum (T=5.11, pFWE<0.05). The neuronal transcription factor MYT1L showed relatively higher expression in AHBA in an overlapping region including the pars opercularis. Large-scale sensory-to-heteromodal functional architecture appears preserved in JFM. However, patients with greater symptom burden show reduced propagation of somatosensory information toward salience-interoceptive regions, suggesting altered multimodal processing. This disruption spatially overlaps with MYT1L expression, pointing towards a developmentally sensitive circuit vulnerability in severe patients.

items.title: Oxidative stress and lipidocentric mechanism of hyperglycemic glycolaldehyde damage to skeletal muscle cells
items.abstract: Currently, diabetes-induced skeletal muscle complications affect over half of diabetic patients yet the pathway by which this hyperglycemic damage occurs has yet to be fully elucidated. As such, the goal of this study is to investigate the hypothesis: Glucose-derived glycolaldehydes, glyoxal and methylglyoxal, formed in hyperglycemia cause damage to the skeletal muscle myoblasts through oxidative stress and formation of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids upon activation of phospholipase A2 (PLA2) and cyclooxygenase (COX). To test this hypothesis skeletal muscle myoblasts, C2C12s, were exposed to various concentrations of glyoxal and methylglyoxal then tested for metabolic activity, reactive oxygen species production, redox status, ATP production, membrane integrity, cellular proliferation, enzyme activity, and loss of mitochondrial lipids. Doses of the agonist at 1 mM and 2 mM showed significant changes in all tested areas and were significantly attenuated by NAC, Ibuprofen, AACOCF3 and metformin. For the first time, these results suggest a plausible pathway by which diabetes-induced skeletal muscle deterioration occurs and identifies possible therapeutic endpoints.

items.title: Designing a Saccharomyces cerevisiae Cell Factory for the Overaccumulation of Tyrosol using Rational Design and Genome-Scale Metabolic Modeling Approaches
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Agrochemistry and Food Technology (IATA-CSIC)
items.abstract: Tyrosol (TyOH) is a phenolic compound with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, naturally present in two Mediterranean products, wine and virgin olive oil, and is the key precursor of Hydroxytyrosol or Salidroside. Its industrial production still relies on chemical synthesis, which conflicts with the EU Green Deal roadmap to transition to a clean, circular, resource-efficient economy by 2050. Thus, moving to a sustainable economy is a priority. Here, we engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a cell factory to produce TyOH. To support this goal, we used ecFactory, a pipeline leveraging enzyme-constrained genome-scale metabolic models (ecGEMs), to predict gene targets, narrowing the candidate list and simplifying experimental validation for strain development. The modifications were tested in a medium composed mainly of glucose with ammonium sulfate as the sole nitrogen source. The final strain reached 876.91 {+/-} 20.37 mg/L in a 0.5 L bioreactor, demonstrating the potential of model-guided engineering for sustainable TyOH production.

items.title: Active exploration generates observer-specific image cues for material identity
items.abstract: When observers interact with an object, each observer generates a different sequence of images. However, which image statistics underlie their perceptual judgments, and whether this self-generated visual input explains what they perceive, remain unclear. We analyzed the first-person recordings of a virtual-reality experiment in which 19 observers judged whether an object was metal or glass while exploring the object with the hand, with the head, with both, and without moving. The object was rendered in two shapes at five levels of physical metallicity and in four illumination environments; every observer saw every stimulus but did so through a different video. Simple image statistics pertaining to the object, to its relation with its surround and to the changes in these properties as the observer explored predicted observers' responses effectively. Critically, when observers disagreed with regard to the same stimulus, their own videos predicted which observer said metal more accurately than chance, and this observer-specific information emerged mainly in the few seconds that preceded the response. The predictive cues identified in this context included the coverage of the optic flow, contrast, highlight coverage, luminance, and the object's luminance and color relative to its surround; furthermore, their importance varied across observers. Thus, active exploration generates different visual evidence for different observers, and their material judgments follow the evidence that they generate.

items.title: Comparative transcriptomic validation of candidate geroprotectors in human iPSC-derived neurons
items.corresponding_institution: Boston University School of Medicine, Center for Regenerative Medicine
items.abstract: The discovery of geroprotectors, defined as interventions that slow aging-related deterioration and preserve function, remains constrained by reliance on lifespan studies. Lifespan studies take years, are costly and resource intensive, and return a whole-organism endpoint dominated in mice by neoplastic death. These studies cannot be readily scaled and do not specify which tissue(s) are protected by geroprotectors. Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cells provide a scalable alternative that enables defined lineages and genetically diverse donors to be studied in parallel. However, reprogramming resets epigenetic age, and whether iPSC-derived cells can report responses relevant to aging has remained unclear. Here, we evaluated eight candidate geroprotectors in iPSC-derived neurons using multiple classes of aging-associated transcriptomic readouts. Aging-associated pathways, including mTORC1 and MEK-ERK signaling, were intact and pharmacologically tunable in these cells. Genetic background accounted for most transcriptional variance, with compound responses differing in magnitude and reproducibility between donors. PI-103 suppressed the mTORC1 signature and increased DCX and BDNF expression, while also inducing genes associated with older age in two independent human excitatory-neuron references. These findings indicate that distinct aging measures capture different dimensions of drug response and that no single readout is sufficient to define geroprotection in our model. Together, these results support iPSC-derived cells as a scalable screening tool for candidate geroprotectors, enabled by the transcriptional aging readouts now available, with the potential to resolve tissue- and donor-dependent responses as additional lineages and donors are incorporated.

items.title: Allele-specific open chromatin analysis revealed allelic bias of alcohol-induced gene expression in human microglia
items.corresponding_institution: Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School
items.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a polygenic disorder. Most AUD-associated variants identified by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are located in non-coding regions, making it challenging to determine which variants are functional and how they contribute to disease-relevant cellular phenotypes. Here, we integrated microglia-specific allele-specific open chromatin (ASoC) mapping, GWAS, eQTLs, differentially expressed genes identified from postmortem human microglia and iPSC-derived microglial-like cells, and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) data from postmortem microglia to prioritize regulatory variants, followed by functional validation using multiple assays. We identified a panel of AUD-associated non-coding variants, particularly rs7307261, as a candidate functional variant that showed regulatory potential. The minor allele (A) of rs7307261 showed higher predicted similarity to binding motifs for E26 transformation-specific (ETS)-family transcription factors, including FLI1 and ELF2, than the G allele. The A allele was also associated with increased CD163 expression in AUD postmortem microglia and in iPSC-derived microglial-like cells after ethanol exposure. Notably, the ethanol-induced CD163 expression was abolished by knocking out rs7307261 or converting rs7307261 A/A to G/G, accompanied by changes in ethanol-induced microglial phagocytic function. Together, our study provides a framework for translating AUD genetic associations into context-specific functional mechanisms by linking non-coding risk variants to target genes and ethanol-induced cellular phenotypes.

items.title: Single-cell transcriptomics atlas of Echinococcus granulosusreveals germinative cell heterogeneity and candidate developmental key genes
items.corresponding_institution: College of Life Sciences, Inner Mongolia University
items.abstract: Cystic echinococcosis is a zoonotic parasitic disease caused by infection with Echinococcus granulosus. Progressive cyst growth can compress host tissues and elicit immune responses. Characterizing the cellular composition and lineage differentiation of E. granulosus protoscoleces may provide insight into the regulation of parasite proliferation and development and facilitate the identification of potential intervention targets. We generated a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of E. granulosus and identified six major cell populations: Germinative cell, Muscle, Neuron, Storage, Tegument,and Cilium. Germinative cells were heterogeneous: some retained an undifferentiated transcriptional profile, whereas others expressed genes associated with differentiated cell types, consistent with the initiation of lineage-associated programs. RNA velocity analysis suggested four potential trajectories, one involving transitions within the undifferentiated population that may contribute to self-renewal and homeostasis, and three showing trends toward distinct lineage-associated subpopulations. A p53 homolog and threonine dehydrogenase tdh were identified as candidate developmental key genes that may contribute to larval growth and development. This study provides a single-cell atlas of E. granulosus protoscoleces and identifies key candidate genes involved in larval development, providing a foundation for future functional studies and the exploration of potential anthelmintic targets.

items.title: mRNAspect: Real-Time Quality Control of Therapeutic mRNA with N1-Methylpseudouridine Bias Correction Using Nanopore Direct RNA Sequencing
items.abstract: Quality attributes of therapeutic mRNA include sequence identity, transcript completeness, and poly(A) tail length. While these attributes require monitoring from development through manufacturing, each needs a separate assay. Nanopore direct RNA sequencing enables rapid quality control because it measures all three on the same molecules within a single run, and the resulting data are available during sequencing. However, N1-methylpseudouridine (m1{Psi}), which often replaces uridine in therapeutic mRNAs, alters the nanopore signal, biasing basecalling and poly(A) estimation. We present mRNAspect, a pipeline combining real-time analysis and m1{Psi} bias correction. mRNAspect includes a fine-tuned basecaller and a poly(A) correction based on the reference sequence. mRNAspect is a packaged macOS app that ingests POD5 or BAM files by watching the MinKNOW output directory as sequencing proceeds. Its graphical user interface shows the latest snapshot of the results, and it writes HTML reports as each input file is processed and a PDF report when the run is finished. When measured on Linux with a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti, each 3-min batch of sequencing (about 5,700 reads) was processed in 38 s. The basecaller was fine-tuned on in vitro transcribed (IVT) constructs and cDNA-IVT libraries. Across 10 m1{Psi} constructs held out from training, the fine-tuned basecaller reduced the error rate from 20.1% to 7.2%, compared with 3.0% for unmodified RNA. A poly(A) correction was fitted to constructs with both modified and unmodified pairs. The correction accounts for the fraction of uridine in the reference sequence and the number of uridines within the 12-nt sequence adjacent to the tail. Across eight constructs, the correction reduced the poly(A) tail length difference between modified and unmodified pairs from up to 9.0 nt to within 1.8 nt.

items.title: Fishing for new immunotherapy compounds to boost innate tumor rejection
items.abstract: Despite significant advances in cancer immunotherapy, tackling immunosuppression remains critical to achieve more effective responses. While developing the zebrafish xenograft model, we found that some human tumors engraft very efficiently ("progressors"), while others are cleared by the host ("regressors"). We showed that this was dependent on innate immunity, which recognizes and eliminates some cancer cells, while others are able to evade and suppress it. This opened an opportunity to perform an in vivo phenotypic drug screen to find compounds that induce clearance by boosting innate-tumor rejection. Zebrafish xenografts of human colorectal (CRC) and breast cancer (BC) that show a high engraftment/low clearance phenotype were used to screen over 500 FDA-approved small-molecule compounds, with tumor clearance serving as the phenotypic readout. The screen identified 23 hit compounds, of which six were effective across both cancer models. Mechanism-of-action enrichment analysis revealed a significant overrepresentation of autonomic nervous system-targeting drugs among the hits, particularly cholinergic ones. Immune profiling in myeloid reporter lines showed that the lead hit, Tiotropium bromide, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, reprograms tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory, anti-tumoral state. Tiotropium significantly increased macrophage phagocytosis, and macrophage depletion completely abolished its pro-clearance activity, establishing these myeloid cells as essential effectors. In a syngeneic CT26 colorectal mouse model, Tiotropium synergized with anti-PD-1 to control tumor growth and improve survival, outperforming all monotherapy arms. This effect was immune-dependent, as it was lost in immunodeficient NSG mice. Together, these findings demonstrate that in vivo phenotypic screening of FDA-approved compounds in zebrafish xenografts is a productive strategy for innate immune drug discovery in cancer. The identification of Tiotropium as a myeloid-reprogramming innate immune primer, together with the unbiased recovery of the neuro-immune axis as a druggable target, opens new avenues for overcoming immunotherapy resistance.

items.title: Targeting ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling enhances IMPDH inhibitor efficacy in mTORC1-driven tumor cells
items.abstract: Uncontrolled activation of the master metabolic regulator Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1) in tumors confers strong dependence on the guanylate nucleotide synthesis enzyme inosine-5'-monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) for tumor cell growth and viability. Clinically approved IMPDH inhibitors reduce the guanylate nucleotide pool available for DNA synthesis in mTORC1-driven tumor cells, resulting in prolonged DNA replication stress and accumulation of DNA damage that culminates in apoptosis. These early molecular events are accompanied by activation of adaptive DNA replication stress response (RSR) and DNA damage response (DDR) pathways. We hypothesized that targeting these adaptive responses could enhance IMPDH inhibitor efficacy. We find that combining IMPDH inhibition with inhibition of the ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling axis increases the efficacy and durability of response in cell models, and in a syngeneic xenograft tumor model of the mTORC1-driven genetic tumor syndrome Tuberous Sclerosis Complex. Mechanistically, abrogating ATR-CHK1-WEE1 signaling during prolonged IMPDH inhibition causes aberrant cell cycle progression, increased DNA double-strand breaks, and formation of micronuclei. Together these findings uncover adaptive mechanisms that restrict IMPDH inhibitor efficacy, informing a combination strategy to improve treatment efficacy, while maintaining selectivity for targeting tumor cells that are driven by uncontrolled mTORC1 activation.

items.title: Constraint-Based Pan-Cancer Metabolic Modeling Identifies Medium-Robust Biomarkers and Broad-Spectrum Anticancer Targets
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Chemical Engineering, National Chung Cheng University
items.abstract: Background: Cancer metabolic reprogramming varies across tumour types and nutrient environments, complicating the identification of robust metabolic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. We developed a constraint based pancancer framework to identify medium robust metabolic alterations and broadly effective candidate enzyme targets. Methods: Transcriptomic profiles from 33 TCGA cancer types were integrated with Recon3D to reconstruct cancer and healthy tissue specific genome scale metabolic models. Parsimonious multiobjective metabolite flow variability analysis was performed under five nutrient conditions to classify differential rates of metabolite synthesis, uptake, and secretion. An extended Anticancer Target Discovery framework incorporating fuzzy multiobjective optimization was employed to evaluate candidate enzyme perturbations based on cancer cell inhibition, ATP suppression, preservation of healthy tissue metabolism, and robustness across nutrient conditions. Findings: The models predicted recurrent increases in cardiolipin-related lipid synthesis and aromatic amino acid metabolism, enhanced uptake of essential amino acids and choline, and elevated lactate secretion across multiple cancer medium combinations. CRLS1 emerged as the most broadly effective predicted enzyme target, satisfying the treatment criteria across all 165 cancer medium combinations, whereas PGS1 and PTPMT1 exhibited broad but incomplete coverage. These findings highlight mitochondrial phospholipid metabolism as a potential shared vulnerability across cancer types and provide testable candidates for metabolomic and experimental validation.

items.title: A tuned topographic map hierarchy formats visual working memory load
items.corresponding_institution: Experimental Psychology, Helmholtz Institute, Utrecht University, Utrecht, Netherlands.
items.abstract: Visual working memory tasks rely on neural systems that scale activity with task load. Traditional models assume higher demands are met by monotonically increasing activity within a single process, implying high informational redundancy across responses. However, theories of cognitive control suggest processing strategies change with task demands, flexibly linking sensory inputs to behavior. Using 7T fMRI and neural encoding models, we hypothesized and confirmed that association cortices format task load-dependent responses using sensory-like neural tuning. We identified populations selectively tuned to specific loads, forming 11 topographic maps per hemisphere hierarchically organized from posterior sensory to anterior executive regions across a fronto-parieto-occipital network. Tuning persisted across performance and trial-order controls, was absent without memory task demands, and predicted behavioral accuracy after load changes. These findings demonstrate that human association cortices distribute task demands using continuously varying processing pathways, adapting sensory-like tuning to decorrelate responses and reduce information redundency during cognitive control.

items.title: GESTATIONAL PROTEIN RESTRICTION PROGRAMS SEXUALLY DIVERGENT BEHAVIORAL AGING IN MICE: EARLY AFFECTIVE VULNERABILITY IN MALES AND LATE-LIFE MNEMONIC PRESERVATION AT A HEDONIC COST IN FEMALES
items.abstract: Maternal protein restriction is a well-established model of developmental programming, yet its consequences for behavior and cognition across the second half of life, and how these differ between sexes, remain poorly characterized. We fed C57BL/6J dams a normal-protein (NP, 17%) or low-protein (LP, 6%) diet throughout gestation and followed male and female offspring with an integrated battery assessing reward sensitivity, locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, social behavior, recognition memory, spatial learning and cognitive flexibility at 12 (middle age) and 18 months (old age). Maternal care was quantified from postnatal days 2 to 9. LP offspring of both sexes were born lighter and caught up by postnatal day 7. LP dams spent more time self-grooming, with longer self-grooming bouts, and took longer to retrieve their pups, whereas licking/grooming, its fragmentation and nursing were unchanged. Middle-aged LP males showed anhedonia-like behavior, anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze, reduced exploration and impaired short-term object recognition; in old age, affective indices normalized, but males became hyperactive and used less efficient search strategies in the Barnes maze. Middle-aged LP females showed hyperactivity, stereotypy and thigmotaxis; at 18 months they developed anhedonia-like behavior yet retained long-term object, social and spatial memory that had declined in aged NP females. A qualitative comparison with a prenatal-stress cohort tested in the same laboratory with the same battery revealed an overlapping, sex- and age-specific signature, particularly for the timing of anhedonia and for late-life memory outcomes. Gestational protein restriction, therefore, programs domain-specific and sexually divergent behavioral aging trajectories rather than uniform cognitive decline. These findings support sex-stratified, life-course designs in fetal programming research.

items.title: Prioritization over certainty: Action planning in visual working memory iscoupled with selective attention, rather than action predictability
items.corresponding_institution: Leibniz Research Centre for Working Environment and Human Factors
items.abstract: When visual information is no longer perceptually available, working memory (WM) allows us to act on sensory representations. But does this guidance require attentional prioritization? We addressed this question by asking participants to remember two oriented bars that were later tested with one predictable and one random probe. This design allowed us to track when a remembered orientation became linked to a specific response hand and whether that link depended on which item was currently prioritized in WM. Response preparation followed prioritization: even when the later response was predictable, no motor preparation emerged while the corresponding item remained latent. Our exploratory analyses showed that prospective action information reduced the need to reprioritize latent items, and that learned stimulus-response mappings generalized across task contexts, suggesting that task-relevant features of visual WM can be partly offloaded onto motor codes. These findings show that active response preparation is coupled with selective attention, while motor representations can also support maintenance in a visual WM task.

items.title: mRNA-1273.262 and mRNA-1283.262 Vaccines Expressing XFG Antigens Neutralize Relevant Circulating Variants
items.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate and causes substantial disease burden as an endemic respiratory pathogen. Vaccination is a key public health measure to ameliorate the effects of COVID-19 disease but requires annual update to match strains that are circulating. Monitoring of circulating virus and characterization of matched candidate vaccines helps to inform which antigens will provide the greatest benefit to public well-being. The 2026-2027 season will leverage XFG as the variant of interest for vaccine production and in vitro and in vivo data was generated preclinically to support this selection. XFG variant vaccines express well in mRNA format as both full-length spike and linked subdomain antigen formats. Animals immunized with these vaccines elicit robust neutralizing responses to relevant JN.1-family virus variants in both primary series and booster models. In future seasons, robust epidemiologically monitoring including viral genome sequencing will improve early detection of relevant variants and subsequent preparation of vaccine antigens.

items.title: Nerve and vascular abnormalities precede loss of corneal transparency in Pax6-haploinsufficient mice
items.abstract: Aniridia-associated keratopathy (AAK), caused by PAX6 haploinsufficiency, progresses from a clinically clear cornea to opacity, neovascularization, and abnormal innervation, but when disease-associated changes first emerge remains unclear. We combined corneal nerve imaging, CD31 immunolabeling, transmission electron microscopy, and RNA sequencing of whole cornea from Pax6Sey-Neu/+mice at postnatal day 3-4, day 15, and adulthood. Corneal transcripts were analyzed using curated axon-guidance, myelination, and vascular/lymphatic gene panels. Mutant corneas showed reduced nerve density and persistent stromal fascicles beginning during the first postnatal week. Peripheral vascular structures were present in both genotypes at birth; these resolved during normal maturation but persisted and extended centrally in mutant corneas by two weeks, before loss of transparency. Transcriptomic analysis identified widespread differences between genotypes while both corneas remained transparent, with the strongest and most coherent changes involving vascular and lymphatic genes. Wild-type corneas silenced an endothelial and lymphatic expression program between postnatal day 15 and adulthood, whereas mutant corneas retained expression of this program. Individual axon-guidance genes differed between genotypes, but axon-guidance did not show program-level expansion in transparent corneas. Compact stromal myelin was restricted to opaque regions. These findings identify early vascular and neural abnormalities that precede corneal opacity and establish that a transparent Pax6-haploinsufficient cornea is already pathologically altered.

items.title: A conserved ubiquitin signalling module controls membrane raft integrity at the neuronal synapse
items.corresponding_institution: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, 71 avenue des Martyrs, 38042, Grenoble, France
items.abstract: Activity-dependent ubiquitination of synaptic proteins is one of the key contributors of synaptic plasticity, along with localized protein synthesis and ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover. Substantial changes in the protein composition occur in the postsynaptic density upon chronic activation or inhibition of primary neurons. Precisely how a large-scale regulation of ensembles of synaptic proteins occurs through the ubiquitin proteasome system remains unknown. MAGE-D1 is a highly conserved protein enriched in brain and its deletion in mice leads to a range of behavioral phenotypes including defects in learning, memory and a complete resistance to cocaine addiction. Here, we found that MAGE-D1 acts as a scaffold bridging the ubiquitin ligase Praja-1 and the deubiquitinase Usp7. This MAGE-D1 signalling module directly interacts with and regulates the levels of Brain acid-soluble protein-1 (BASP1) which is a key component and stabilizer of neuronal membrane rafts. Disruption of MAGE-D1 complex function or chemical inhibition of Usp7 in mice results in resistance to cocaine-induced locomotor sensitization accompanied by specific degradation of oligomeric BASP1 and other key synaptic proteins in the postsynaptic density of mice thalamus. As a result, loss of MAGE-D1 in differentiated neurons leads to a dramatic disorganization of neuronal membrane rafts and anomalies in the synaptic membrane protein landscape. Finally, we mapped the structural architecture of the human MAGE-D1/Praja-1/Usp7 complex revealing the basis for the scaffolding nature of MAGE-D1. In summary, we discovered a conserved synaptic ubiquitin signalling network mediated by a protein complex that localizes to the synapse and regulates structures of membrane rafts and actin cytoskeleton.

items.title: DDB2 localizes to the nucleolus to mediate oxaliplatin resistance in colorectal cancer
items.abstract: Despite the widespread use of platinum drugs in cancer therapy, defining their mechanisms of action and predicting clinical outcomes remain challenging. Unlike cisplatin, which kills cells mainly through the DNA damage response, oxaliplatin toxicity is driven largely by nucleolar stress, yet how cells cope with this stress remains poorly understood. A nucleotide excision repair protein, damage-specific DNA binding protein 2 (DDB2), protects cells from oxaliplatin but not cisplatin, suggesting that it may preferentially engage oxaliplatin adducts. Using single-molecule analysis of DNA-binding proteins from nuclear extracts, we show that DDB2 binds both oxaliplatin and cisplatin intrastrand adducts. Oxaliplatin, but not cisplatin, drives progressive accumulation of DDB2 in nucleoli, pointing to a role at sites of oxaliplatin-induced nucleolar stress. The repair-deficient xeroderma pigmentosum group E K244E variant localizes to nucleoli but fails to rescue oxaliplatin sensitivity of DDB2-knockout cells, indicating that repair activity, not nucleolar localization alone, is required for protection. In colorectal cancer (CRC), elevated DDB2 levels correlate with higher oxaliplatin IC50, are higher in tumors than adjacent normal tissue by immunohistochemistry, and DDB2 transcript associates with non-response and shorter progression-free survival in FOLFOX-treated patients. Pharmacological inactivation or degradation of DDB2 synergizes with oxaliplatin, offering a biomarker-driven strategy to overcome chemoresistance.

items.title: CSF Boundary Disruption and Tumor-Dependent Patterns of Medulloblastoma Metastasis
items.abstract: Background: Leptomeningeal metastasis is the major cause of mortality in medulloblastoma, yet the mechanisms that facilitate dissemination are poorly resolved. Here, we leveraged preclinical models to define metastatic topology, the anatomical distribution and organization of disseminated disease across craniospinal compartments and ask how topology is influenced by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) access, primary tumor anatomy, and tumor biology. Methods: Orthotopic D425 xenograft models were used to manipulate primary tumor geometry, defined by anatomical position of primary tumors within the cerebellum relative to CSF facing boundaries. Longitudinal bioluminescence, survival, primary growth architecture at the tumor host interface, CSF boundary breach, and craniospinal metastatic distribution were quantified. Additional medulloblastoma models MED411, MED2112, and CHLA-01-MED were implanted at a common midline cerebellar location to assess tumor-intrinsic contributions to metastatic topology. Results: While primary tumor geometry altered disease progression and survival, it did not significantly alter metastasis distribution. Strikingly, growth architecture and primary tumor burden correlated with dissemination. Despite their large size, circumscribed tumors frequently remained localized, whereas smaller, disruptive primary growth architecture was strongly associated with boundary breach, intracranial, and spinal dissemination. Conversely, when anatomical origin was held constant, distinct medulloblastoma models generated significantly different metastatic topologies. Conclusions: Disruption of CSF-facing anatomical boundaries is associated with distant dissemination, whereas the distribution of established metastatic disease differs substantially among medulloblastoma models despite standardized implantation conditions. These findings distinguish anatomical factors associated with dissemination from tumor-dependent patterns of metastatic colonization and establish an experimental framework for investigating the mechanisms underlying metastatic topology.

items.title: Archetypal analysis provides interpretable mixture representations of microbiome community structure
items.corresponding_institution: Genetic Heritage Group, Program in Biology, New York University Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, UAE
items.abstract: Microbiome studies routinely reduce high-dimensional community profiles to a small number of coordinates for visualization and comparison. Ordination methods are powerful for detecting compositional differences, but their axes are often difficult to translate into explicit microbial community configurations; conversely, hard clustering can impose discrete states on variation that is frequently continuous. Here we evaluate Archetypal Analysis (AA) as an intermediate representation in which each microbiome is expressed as a convex combination of a small number of data-supported extreme community profiles. Across three applications, AA recovered biologically recognizable structure while preserving graded variation among samples. In a multi-biospecimen human microbiome dataset, different sample-source categories occupied characteristic regions of archetype space, while stool samples were represented by heterogeneous mixtures of archetypal profiles. In an early-life gut microbiome dataset, archetype usage changed systematically with age, describing microbial succession as changing contributions from community endpoints. In domestic dogs spanning forager, agrarian, pastoralist, urban, and industrialized lifestyles, groups showed characteristic but non-discrete combinations of archetypes, supporting generality across host species and ecological contexts. Across the displayed K-sensitivity analyses, the principal sample-source and early-life organization remained recognizable as model resolution changed, while repeated initialization and resampling analyses recovered similar archetypal structure. Held-out samples projected onto fixed training-derived archetypes retained metadata-associated organization within each dataset. Bray-Curtis principal coordinates analysis recovered the same broad biological structure, indicating that the value of AA is interpretive rather than simply greater separation, while taxa prioritized by AA retained substantial predictive information relative to equally sized random taxon sets. Together, these results support AA as a complementary microbiome representation that connects low-dimensional sample coordinates directly to interpretable taxonomic profiles and provides a natural framework for describing ecological states, gradients, and transitions without hard cluster assignments.

items.title: The emergence and neural organisation of facial-expression information during ultra-brief vision
items.abstract: A glimpse lasting only a few milliseconds can convey meaningful information about a face, but how the brain transforms such minimal input into stable representations of facial expression and conscious experience remains unclear. Across two experiments using ultra-brief face presentations, we combined hierarchical psychophysical modelling, multivariate EEG decoding, and information-theoretic measures to characterise this transformation. Extending previously reported findings, hierarchical modelling quantified distinct exposure-dependent trajectories for intact-face localisation and expression identification, providing a behavioural calibration of weak, intermediate, and stronger perceptual evidence. The critical neural transition occurred between 4.4 and 6.2 ms. At 4.4 ms, expression sensitivity was behaviourally detectable, but neural expression patterns did not reliably generalise to faces excluded from classifier training. At 6.2 ms, previously observed emotion-related ERP differences were accompanied by expression representations that generalised across faces and locally detectable emotion information during the early posterior negativity (EPN) interval. Subjective clarity tracked location-related neural evidence more consistently than expression-specific evidence, indicating that awareness did not simply mirror the emerging expression representation. The degree to which early centroparietal activity statistically predicted later occipital activity differed between emotional and neutral faces as exposure increased, indicating that the relationship between successive neural responses was reorganised. Thus, a few additional milliseconds of visual input did not merely strengthen facial-expression processing; they transformed weak evidence that did not reliably generalise across faces into more stable, generalisable, behaviourally relevant, and distributed neural information.

items.title: PMRIPrep: automated preprocessing and quantification of DSC and DCE MRI
items.abstract: While dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) MRI measures hemodynamics and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI characterizes vascular permeability, quantitative values from both modalities remain processing-dependent. We present PMRIPrep, a Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) App for automated DSC and DCE preprocessing and quantification. PMRIPrep adapts to available acquisitions and metadata, integrates both modalities within a session, and supports four DSC deconvolution methods and four DCE pharmacokinetic models. In DSC simulations with 4% cerebral blood volume and signal-to-noise ratio 50, pooled median absolute cerebral blood flow error was 13-19% across methods. Median Ktrans bias remained [≤]2% across four model-matched DCE configurations over 0-10% noise. End-to-end OSIPI analyses yielded DCE accuracy and clinical test-retest repeatability scores of 0.85 and 0.85, respectively. Outputs follow BIDS-Derivatives conventions and include machine-readable provenance and visual quality-control reports. PMRIPrep is freely available as a containerized application.

items.title: Self-generated action shapes theta phase alignment at encoding and later recollection
items.abstract: Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses. These findings link self-generated action to the timing of encoding-related oscillations and to subsequent recollection. The association between later posterior theta alignment and Remember-Know discrimination is consistent with a role for theta phase coordination in associative binding.

items.title: Genetically Encoded Photodecaging of Asparagine Enables Protein Function Control and Time-Resolved N-Glycosylation
items.abstract: Asparagine contributes to protein function through its polar carboxamide side chain and serves as the acceptor residue for N-linked glycosylation, yet temporally controlling these roles directly through the side-chain carboxamide remains challenging. Here, we report the genetic encoding of N4-(2-nitrobenzyl)-L-asparagine (ONBN), a photocaged asparagine that regenerates the native side-chain carboxamide upon 365 nm irradiation. Engineered aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase/tRNA pairs enabled site-specific ONBN incorporation into proteins in Escherichia coli and mammalian cells. Photodecaging restored Renilla luciferase activity and activated TRAF6 polyubiquitination mediated by UBE2N in living cells. Beyond active-site residues, we further developed CAGE-proxN, using computationally guided proximal caging to optically activate firefly luciferase. Finally, ONBN incorporation at the acceptor position of an N-glycosylation sequon enabled light-triggered initiation and time-resolved monitoring of post-translational glycan installation on an endoplasmic reticulum-targeted reporter. Variation of the -2 flanking residue revealed sequence-dependent differences in apparent glycosylation kinetics. This work extends genetically encoded photocontrol to the asparagine carboxamide and provides a platform for investigating asparagine-dependent protein functions and the temporal regulation of N-glycosylation in living cells.

items.title: An isogenic platform to model the impact of sex chromosome and donor genotype in hiPSC-derived vascular smooth muscle cells
items.abstract: Monosomy-X results in Turner Syndrome (TS), which beyond its cardinal height and reproductive phenotypes, spans incompletely penetrant cardiovascular phenotypes, including bicuspid valve, hypoplastic left-sided heart syndrome and aortic coarctation. These congenital heart defects (CHD) conspire with hypertension to dilate the ascending aorta, which can progress to rupture and drive early mortality in TS. Genetic contributors to incompletely penetrant phenotypes in TS remain only partially explored, thus complicating risk stratification. To begin addressing this challenge in donor-specific in-vitro models, we derived monosomy-X human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) alongside isogenic euploid control lines from donors mosaic for the second sex chromosome. In embryonic-origin specific vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs) derived from these hiPSCs, monosomy-X reveals donor-specific cellular and transcriptomic effects, with expression changes in one donor panel enriched in genes previously implicated in coronary artery disease and ascending aorta diameter. Polygenic risk scores (PGS) for cardiovascular traits mirror this transcriptomic enrichment, and suggest PGS analysis may help to prioritize hiPSC lines for in-vitro modeling of incompletely-penetrant traits related to TS-associated aortopathy.

items.title: A comprehensive Drosophila toolkit reveals context-dependent functional hierarchies across RasG12X variants in vivo
items.corresponding_institution: MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS), London, UK
items.abstract: KRAS is a GTPase regulating key signalling processes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, growth and survival. KRAS is the most prevalent oncogene in human cancers, often acquiring a point mutation at Glycine 12 (G12). Although several possible amino acid substitutions occur at this hotspot in humans, most animal cancer models often examine only a single or limited subset of G12X variants, restricting our understanding of their distinct biological effects. Here, we describe a novel transgenic toolkit in Drosophila melanogaster comparing the most frequently observed oncogenic G12X variants (G12A, G12C, G12D, G12R, G12S, G12V), and evaluate these across multiple developmental and tumour contexts in vivo. Interestingly, we demonstrate how the phenotypic strength of each G12X variant differs significantly depending on the biological context, highlighting the importance of considering these point mutations systematically. Overall, our comprehensive RasG12X toolkit provides a powerful and versatile platform to explore the dysregulation of KRAS in vivo, serving as a valuable resource enabling unprecedented opportunities to investigate variant- and context-specific mechanisms of oncogenic signalling with direct relevance to cancer biology and therapy.

items.title: ceTDP: A Practical Tutorial on Valid and Quantitative Cluster-Extent Inference in Neuroimaging
items.abstract: We introduce ceTDP, a two-stage framework for cluster-extent inference in neuroimaging that extends conventional random field theory-based and permutation-based methods. In contrast to standard cluster inference, which yields binary significance, ceTDP additionally quantifies the proportion of truly active voxels within clusters using the true discovery proportion (TDP). The method is built on closed testing and provides strong family-wise error rate control while remaining consistent with standard cluster inference. The framework operates in two stages: estimation of a cluster-extent threshold, followed by computation of the TDP lower bound. Two complementary procedures are provided: a conservative, statistically guaranteed TDP lower bound (ceTDP-cons) and a heuristic approach for obtaining a potentially tighter estimate of the TDP lower bound (ceTDP-heur). Together, they enable both rigorous inference and improved sensitivity in cluster-level analysis.

items.title: An ancient Hippo-dystrophin axis controls cortical stability and multicellular interactions in a close unicellular relative of animals
items.abstract: How the protein complexes and signal transduction pathways that regulate animal physiology and human disease emerged over evolutionary time remains poorly understood. The dystrophin-dystroglycan complex (DGC), whose disruption causes muscular dystrophy in humans, is best known for its role in maintaining muscle integrity and was previously thought to have originated in animals. Here we show that Capsaspora owczarzaki, a close unicellular relative of animals, encodes core DGC components- including a bona fide dystroglycan ortholog- as critical downstream targets of the Hippo pathway. Loss of Capsaspora dystrophin (coDystrophin) destabilizes the cortical actin cytoskeleton, causes excessive membrane blebbing, and produces flattened, irregularly shaped multicellular aggregates, all of which phenocopy loss of coYki. Conversely, coDystrophin overexpression rescues the cytoskeletal defects of coYki mutant cells, identifying coDystrophin as a key effector of Hippo signaling. Despite extensive rearrangement of dystrophin domain architecture during animal evolution, a human microdystrophin partially rescues coDystrophin mutant cells, revealing deep functional conservation. These findings show that core DGC components predate animals and indicate that the complex's ancestral role was not muscle-specific but lay in maintaining cortical cytoskeletal integrity under the control of an ancient Hippo-regulated genetic module.

items.title: Deep Learning Prediction of DNA Damage Response Protein Signaling from H&E Histopathology and Reverse-Phase Protein Arrays in Pan-Gynecologic and Breast Cancers
items.abstract: Defects in homologous recombination and the DNA damage response (DDR) make gynecologic and breast tumors sensitive to platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, but identifying them requires costly genomic testing that reads permanent genomic scars rather than current pathway activity. Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides are available for nearly every patient. This project asked whether H&E morphology carries information about functional DDR protein signaling across five cancer types in a single model. We matched 1,673 diagnostic whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to Level 4 reverse-phase protein array (RPPA) data for 1,527 patients with breast (BRCA, n = 858), endometrial (UCEC, n = 403), cervical (CESC, n = 146), ovarian (OV, n = 72), and uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS, n = 48) tumors. Slides were tiled at 0.5 m/px and Macenko-normalized, yielding 20.4 million tiles. Tiles were embedded with two frozen pathology foundation models, UNI2-h and Virchow2. A gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) network jointly regressed six RPPA pathway scores, including a DNA_damage composite of 11 DDR proteins. Performance was assessed by out-of-fold Spearman correlation under 5-fold, cancer-type-stratified, site-grouped cross-validation and compared against a baseline that predicts each patient's cancer-type mean. Predicted DNA_damage correlated with measured values ({rho} = 0.43 for both encoders) and exceeded the cancer-type baseline ({rho} = 0.31; {Delta} {rho} = +0.13). The signal held within cancer types (within-type {rho} = 0.29 for UNI2-h, 0.30 for Virchow2). With the original UNI encoder, it survived site-held-out folds with residualized targets (within-type {rho} = 0.26), and it vanished when targets were shuffled within cancer type (within-type {rho} [≤] 0.00 for all three encoders). All six pathway scores were predicted above baseline; Cell_cycle was strongest ({rho} {approx} 0.59). In interpretability analyses, the top 10 attention tiles per slide contained more tumor (+1.8 SD), larger tumor nuclei (+1.0 to +1.3 SD), and fewer lymphocytes (-0.6 SD) than the bottom 10 tiles; 13 of 14 morphometric features differed (q < 0.05). Attention agreed with Integrated Gradients (median {rho} {approx} 0.70). Routine H&E contains a moderate, reproducible signal of DDR protein abundance beyond cancer type, concentrated in tumor-dense regions with enlarged nuclei. Separating this signal from proliferation and predicting phosphorylated CHK1 and CHK2 directly are the next steps toward a functional, slide-based DDR biomarker.

items.title: Sustained LDL-C Lowering Reveals Selective Expansion of Fibroblast Subpopulations with Distinct Regulatory and Matrix Programs During Atherosclerosis Remodeling
items.abstract: Background: Smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and SMC-derived cells contribute to atherosclerotic plaque stability through matrix production and fibrous cap formation. Recent studies have also identified distinct fibroblast populations in atherosclerotic lesions, but how these populations respond to sustained LDL-C lowering and contribute to plaque remodeling remains poorly understood. Methods: We combined serial histological assessment, SMC lineage tracing, and single-cell RNA sequencing to examine vascular stromal cell and lesion structural responses during 20 weeks of sustained LDL-C lowering in mice with established atherosclerosis. Regulatory network analysis and computational perturbation predictions were supported by KLF3 and FOXD1 silencing in cultured mouse and human aortic fibroblasts. Results: LDL-C lowering led to rapid reductions in macrophage content and cleaved gasdermin D, followed by decreased necrotic core area and increased collagen content and fibrous cap thickness, with minimal change in lesion area. During this remodeling, SMC-derived cell populations changed little. In striking contrast, CD26 and FMOD fibroblast subtypes increased by 5 weeks and remained elevated through 20 weeks, with increased fibroblast-associated signals in the intima and fibrous cap. These populations showed distinct matrix programs, with ECM glycoprotein and regulatory programs enriched in CD26 fibroblasts and collagen and proteoglycan programs in FMOD fibroblasts. Regulatory network analysis identified KLF3 and FOXD1 as candidate master regulators of CD26 and FMOD fibroblasts, respectively. Silencing either factor reduced selected matrix-associated and proliferation transcripts and impaired scratch closure in mouse and human aortic fibroblasts, while KLF3 silencing also increased selected inflammatory genes. Exploratory human genetic analyses identified associations of KLF3-region and FOXD1 variation with coronary artery disease. Conclusions: These findings reveal fibroblast subtype-specific responses during sustained LDL-C lowering and identify KLF3 and FOXD1 as candidate transcriptional regulators of fibroblast matrix-associated and inflammatory functions relevant to plaque remodeling and stabilization.

items.title: Ecological characterisation of frequency-domain local field potential biomarkers in essential tremor.
